📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that calling a judge a vulgar name is rude, but it does not amount to criminal contempt, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court recently found. (Image from Shutterstock).

The criminal contempt conviction of a courtroom spectator who called a judge a vulgar name after she ruled against a motion that his acquaintance filed was recently vacated by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.

Basile Outlaw spent 30 days in jail after the 2022 incident involving Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington, Reason reports.

“What did you say?” Covington responded to his remark, according to the article.

“Never mind, I’m leaving,” Outlaw said.

He claims that he later came back to apologize and was taken into custody, Reason reports.

In a recent development, in December 2023, the Pennsylvania Superior Court upheld Outlaw’s conviction. The state supreme court reversed and vacated the conviction in late October, finding that while what Outlaw did was rude, it wasn’t enough for criminal contempt.

The majority opinion cited an earlier finding involving a pro se party in a custody dispute calling the judge a vulgar term.

Industry observers note that here, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court also reversed a criminal contempt conviction for the party. In both cases, the state supreme court found, the outbursts amounted to momentary breaks in the proceedings, not significant disruptions.

    Rights Defender in Central African Republic Dies

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70.
    • It has been revealed that tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986.
    • For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades.

    It has been revealed that tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup.

    For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by. By the early 1990s, Tiangaye was one of the leading Central African human rights advocates and served as the Bar Association president.

    It has been revealed that in 1996 he was the lead defense council for Jean-Paul Akayesu before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. Human Rights Watch strongly advocated for the prosecution of Akayesu hailing his 1998 conviction as a historic international precedent. I once discussed the seminal conviction with Tiangaye and he reiterated that a good lawyer must be willing to defend clients and insist on due process, even in highly charged circumstances.

    Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, he spoke out for judicial independence and democratic governance. This often put him at odds with the government. But threats, he said, came with the job.

    It has been revealed that he regularly ended up at the heart of national politics. Following Bozizé's successful coup, Tiangaye helped draft the 2004 Constitution. In January 2013, then-president Bozizé appointed Tiangaye prime minister amidst national turmoil. He remained in the position after Seleka seized Bangui and committed widespread abuses. Tiangaye despised the Seleka’s crimes, he told me, and he resigned.

    He returned to legal practice and his passion: defending the Constitution. He became an outspoken critic of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra's efforts to remove presidential term limits, insisting on constitutional safeguards and political pluralism.

    His death is both a professional and personal loss for Human Rights Watch. More importantly, it occurs as independent voices and institutions remain under pressure in the Central African Republic. I spoke with him just last week about detained activists. I wish I asked how he would like to be remembered. I imagine he would have insisted that we not focus on the individual, but on his commitment to the rule of law and human rights—Tiangaye’s ultimate legacy.

    US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa.

    Discrimination, Lack of Economic Autonomy and Violence Against Women in Cameroon.

    Georgetown's Counterclaims Against Professor Fired for "Sexual Misconduct" Can Go Forward

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From Judge Amy Berman Jackson (D.D.C.) yesterday in Egolf v.
    • Plaintiff David Egolf was a tenured associate professor at defendant Georgetown University ….
    • Egolf filed suit against Georgetown and certain University officials, claiming that the second investigation violated Title IX, Georgetown's Faculty Handbook, and the 2015 settlement agreement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From Judge Amy Berman Jackson (D.D.C.) yesterday in Egolf v. Georgetown Univ.:.

    Plaintiff David Egolf was a tenured associate professor at defendant Georgetown University …. In 2015, after an investigation into an internal complaint lodged against Egolf by a Georgetown student, the parties entered into a settlement agreement that placed rules on Egolf's conduct in return for his continued employment at the University. In 2023, following a second report by a recent Georgetown graduate, the University completed another investigation into Egolf and his conduct.

    Egolf filed suit against Georgetown and certain University officials, claiming that the second investigation violated Title IX, Georgetown's Faculty Handbook, and the 2015 settlement agreement. Georgetown has answered the complaint and has filed a counterclaim alleging that Egolf breached the 2015 settlement agreement when he engaged in conduct that violated numerous provisions of the contract. Georgetown seeks compensatory damages and a declaratory judgment….

    Recent findings suggest that according to Georgetown, on September 20, 2013, a student accused Egolf of sexual harassment. Egolf was placed on administrative leave with pay while the University reviewed the student's complaint. The University's Office of Institutional Diversity, Equity, and Affirmative Action ("IDEAA") investigated the claim and, on May 9, 2014, issued a Notice of Findings in which it found, in part, that Egolf:.

    violated the University's Policy Statement on Harassment and Sexual Harassment by making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature in violation of the policy; engaged in prohibited retaliation against the student; and failed to recognize and ignored the principle underlying [the University's Policy on Consensual Sexual Relationships], which prohibits participation in a professional relationship with a student where there is a conflict of interest.

    Moreover, with respect to the University's alcohol policy and Faculty Handbook, IDEAA found that:.

    (1) [Egolf] served, offered, gave, purchased, and provided alcohol on multiple occasions to [the student] and his roommate, both of whom were underage, and (2) [Egolf] engaged in unfair treatment of [the student], engaged in unprofessional conduct; abused his academic authority over [the student]; engaged in a personal relationship for his own gratification; improperly shared other student information with [the student]; and allowed his objectivity as a professor to be compromised.

    The Notice of Findings recommended that the University consider "the most serious academic and employment sanctions," glitch a no-contact directive between Egolf and the student, and require Egolf to remain off campus and have no contact with University students pending the University's decision regarding sanctions. Egolf appealed IDEAA's findings and recommendations, which were later upheld by the University's Equal Opportunity Examining Board on September 14, 2014.

    According to recent reports, according to Georgetown, on October 14, 2014, University Provost Robert Groves issued a Termination Letter to Egolf, and then on December 3, 2014, Egolf filed a Notice of Grievance challenging IDEAA's findings and Provost Groves's termination decision. After a closed and confidential conciliation process, on October 15, 2015, the parties entered into an agreement ("2015 Agreement") which permitted Egolf's reinstatement subject to "strict and continuing behavioral restrictions." The 2015 Agreement:.

    The 2015 Agreement also stated that if Egolf had "any questions as to whether a relationship with a student is appropriate," he was required to "immediately disclose the relationship to his chair or dean." ….

    In May 2023, Robert Roe, one of Egolf's former students, started a postbaccalaureate program at Georgetown under Egolf's supervision. While in school, Roe took multiple classes taught by Egolf, served as his Research Assistant over the course of a summer, and was his academic advisee. Georgetown alleges that, on or about July 19, 2023, Roe contacted defendant Samantha Berner, Georgetown's Title IX Coordinator and Director of Title IX Compliance, to raise concerns regarding Egolf's conduct, which Roe characterized as "grooming." ….

    According to recent reports, according to Georgetown, on May 6, 2024, IDEAA released a confidential investigative report stating that there was "sufficient evidence under a preponderance of the evidence standard to substantiate a finding" of Egolf's sexual misconduct, resulting in violations of University policy, the Faculty Handbook, and the 2015 Agreement…. The IDEAA investigative report found that Egolf maintained a "personal and social relationship with a student that he advised, including frequent non-academic communications, social outings, private meetings, and sustained personal involvement extending beyond appropriate faculty-student boundaries." Egolf admitted the truth of certain factual findings in his appeal by stating, "[t]his statement is true," including:.

    It has been revealed that according to Georgetown, in Egolf's appeal, he further admitted that he and Roe had meals together "about once a month" at a restaurant near the University where they would discuss academic and personal topics. The meals initially included other students and alumni but later became more often one-on-one. Egolf also allegedly admitted that:.

    According to recent reports, [Egolf] invited Mr. [Roe] to spend the night at his house after their celebration of Mr. [Roe]'s graduation, since they expected to drink and it would be late. [Egolf] invited Mr. [Roe] to spend the night at his house after they went to see the Lion King so that he would not have to drive to Mr. [Roe]'s home in Reston and back the night immediately preceding when Mr. [Roe] was already slated to go to [Egolf]'s home for their graduation celebration.

    According to Georgetown, Egolf stated in his appeal that he and the student consumed three-and-a-half bottles of champagne together that same evening; he left the door slightly ajar when he went into the bathroom; he told Roe stories about being propositioned by a student and finding a student naked on his couch; he made a joke about his college friend's genitalia; and he participated in conduct related to a drinking game.

    Georgetown also alleges that Egolf provided Roe with private study sessions, inflated his grades in a manner inconsistent with academic evaluation standards, and substantially assisted in drafting a portion of his undergraduate thesis and grant application.

    Moreover, Egolf allegedly texted Roe that, upon Roe's graduation, Egolf would be able to tell him "all of the crazy stories I've hinted at" and did share the explicit stories following graduation; engaged in discussions about nudity and other sexual topics; made a joke involving genitalia; and teased Roe while offering to help remove his pants. Finally, Georgetown alleges that Egolf failed to disclose the nature or extent of his relationship with Roe to any University administrator as required by the 2015 Agreement…..

    Egolf was eventually fired. Before the firing (but after he was put on paid leave), he sued, alleging Title IX retaliation, breach of contract, and other matters, and Georgetown counterclaimed, "alleging breach of the 2015 Agreement and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing," and seeking compensatory damages for the costs of various proceedings (including the legal costs of defending the lawsuit). The court allowed the claims to go forward; an excerpt:.

    According to recent reports, to state a claim for breach of contract, "it is enough for the plaintiff to describe the terms of the alleged contract and the nature of the defendant's breach." Contrary to Egolf's assertions, a plaintiff need not allege damages caused by the breach to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss…. Georgetown claims that Egolf violated the agreement by:.

    Finally, Georgetown identifies the five specific provisions of the 2015 Agreement they allege that Egolf violated.

    Even if Egolf is correct that Georgetown must allege damages to state a claim, the Court does not find that, on the face of the counterclaim, consequential damages were outside the contemplation of the parties at the time of the contract…. [P]aragraph 11 of the Agreement demonstrates that the parties expressly contemplated the possibility of litigation. Ex. A at 11 ("Any breach, or actions taken upon breach, of the Agreement by either party may also be enforced by filing suit, or seeking an injunction, in a court of competent jurisdiction"). Resolving all reasonable inferences in Georgetown's favor, the Court does not find that legal damages were beyond the contemplation of the 2015 Agreement.

    Brian Drockton and Henry Adam Platt (Saul Ewing LLP) represent Georgetown.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As world leaders recently gathered in Phnom Penh to celebrate the 20th Francophonie Summit with the theme of peace and shared prosperity, French President Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to call publicly for an investigation into the killing of former Cambodian lawmaker and French citizen Lim Kimya. It was a rare public rebuke of the Cambodian government by a foreign leader.

    A gunman killed Kimya in Bangkok, Thailand in January 2025. Kimya had served as a parliament member with the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party before its 2017 dissolution.

    A Thai court convicted the gunman, Ekkalak Paenoi, in October 2025 and issued arrest warrants for two Cambodian suspects, Ly Ratanakraksmey and Pich Kimsrin, both of whom have connections to high-ranking Cambodian officials. The Cambodian government—like many of its neighbors in Southeast Asia—is increasingly persecuting activists abroad.

    Sources indicate that the Cambodian government has yet to acknowledge the arrest warrants or start an impartial investigation. Both men remain at large. France has issued Interpol Red Notices for them on charges of complicity in premeditated murder.

    According to recent reports, macron’s raising Kimya’s murder during a joint press conference with Prime Minister Hun Manet sends a strong message that the French government is taking Cambodian authorities’ attacks on activists abroad seriously. The Cambodian government should heed the call and independently and impartially investigate the murder.

    In a recent development, but political repression by the Cambodian government runs deeper than one case. Ahead of 2027 local elections, the authorities are escalating their crackdown on the long suppressed political opposition. Young activists in particular, such as the five imprisoned Mother Nature Cambodia environmental activists, have been punished with baseless treason charges and lengthy prison sentences. Concerned governments should publicly and privately urge Cambodian authorities to release the more than 100 Cambodians presently imprisoned for exercising their fundamental freedoms.

    According to recent reports, human Rights Watch was among the local and international organizations that pressed Cambodian authorities to release the Mother Nature activists and others ahead of the Francophonie Summit. The ruling Cambodian People’s Party, which exerts complete control over the country’s courts, was apparently unbothered by these efforts.

    Other foreign leaders should amplify Macron’s message and publicly call on Cambodia’s government to reopen the space for the political opposition and respect the fundamental rights of all Cambodians, both at home and abroad.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 12, 2026, 11:16 am CST.

    Alina Habba Mildon at the White House in March 2025. (Photo by Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post).

    The Upcoming Jersey Office of Attorney Ethics filed a disciplinary complaint Tuesday against Alina Habba Mildon—a former personal lawyer to President Donald Trump and a former acting U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey—over her role in settling a 2021 sexual harassment dispute at the Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey, where she was a paying member.

    Reuters reported Wednesday that regulators alleged that Mildon steered a 21-year-old club employee, Alice Bianco, into a $15,000 settlement of misconduct claims against her boss.

    According to Reuters, Mildon allegedly persuaded Bianco to stop communicating with her attorney, potentially confusing Bianco into thinking that Mildon was acting as her lawyer. The complaint also alleged that Mildon undervalued the claims in a way that benefited the club and did not disclose her financial ties to it. Mildon became a personal lawyer to Trump soon afterward.

    In a recent development, bianco later hired attorney Nancy Smith, who sued the club in 2023 and settled for $400,000. In a statement to Reuters, Smith claimed that Mildon “got ​my client to terminate her lawyer, accept a ridiculously low settlement, ​and agree to an illegal nondisclosure agreement, silencing her.”.

    Smith added that she thought that Mildon’s “numerous ethics violations in that scenario should result in disbarment.”.

    Mildon’s attorney, Kim Ringler, told Reuters that “the complaint ⁠starts a long process for resolving concerns about conduct that took place more than five years ago.”.

    Sources indicate that the complaint adds to Mildon’s recent troubles. A federal judge ruled last year that her appointment as New Jersey’s top federal prosecutor was unlawful. Trump also publicly called a $50 million contract that she obtained while at the Department of Justice “unacceptable,” and the New York Times reported Tuesday that she has since lost it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Pew Research Center has published a comprehensive survey about population growth within the world religions between 2020 and 2070. The results are worth a careful study to forecast the future religious landscape in the United States, and how those numbers will affect debates about religious liberty. Here is a summary:.

    The United States is expected to follow roughly the same pattern of religious change as the overall North American region.5 By 2070, Christians are expected to decline to less than half of the U.S. population, while religiously unaffiliated people will rise to about 41%. And Jews – who were the country's third-largest religious group in 2020 – will be outnumbered by both Muslims and Hindus in 2070 if recent demographic trends continue.

    The numbers concerning Jews are also significant:.

    As of 2020, Pew Research Center estimates there were about 15 million Jews by religion around the world, 12.5 million of whom lived in Israel and the United States. By the Center's projections, Israel alone will hold the majority of the world's Jews within a few decades.

    If recent demographic trends continue, Israel will be home to 62% of the global Jewish population in 2070, up from 46% in 2020. During this 50-year time span, the number of Jews living in Israel is forecast to grow from 6.8 million to 11.1 million, due primarily to what demographers call "natural increase": the number of births exceeding the number of deaths in a population.

    Industry observers note that I've written on this blog before that I can see a future where my family and I will have to move to Israel. The events of the last election make that outcome seem just-that-much-more likely. And remember, the persecution of Jews will always be a precursor to persecution of other faiths.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately, debates about religious liberty will look very different as the composition of religious group changes. I would note that at the recent Federalist Society convention, there was a brief mention about the risks of Shariah Law--a topic that I can't ever recall being discussed on a FedSoc platform. This issue will soon get even hotter in Texas as the government continues to shift.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Journalists, activists and political opponents who fled Burkina Faso to escape the junta’s repression now risk arrest and prosecution abroad, as the country’s judicial authorities pursue dozens of individuals over alleged terrorism-related offenses.

    It has been revealed that burkina Faso Prosecutor General Désiré Sawadogo revealed on November 13 that a special court handling terrorism-related offenses had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities. All those targeted exposed serious military abuses during counterinsurgency operations and include exiled journalists critical of the junta, among them Ahmed Newton Barry, Issaka Lingani, Inoussa Ouédraogo, Adama Ouedraogo, and Abdoulaye Barry; exiled social media activist Naïm Touré; former foreign affairs minister Alpha Barry, and international journalist Wassim Nasr. They face various charges, including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism.

    According to recent reports, burkina Faso sent international arrest warrants and extradition requests to Côte d’Ivoire, France, and the United States, remarked Sawadogo. He added that Burkina Faso asked the United States to use Meta to identify and prosecute Facebook page administrators accused of promoting terrorism.

    It has been revealed that the authorities are using counterterrorism laws to target critical voices and restrict independent reporting on military abuses. The extradition requests extend political repression beyond Burkina Faso’s borders, placing critics who sought protection abroad at risk of arrest, forced return, and further abuse. The government’s recent decision to reinstate capital punishment for offenses including terrorism, high treason, and espionage is also of grave concern.

    Since seizing power in a September 2022 coup, the junta has restricted fundamental rights through media bans, suspension of unions and civil society organizations, dissolution of political parties, enforced disappearances, and the unlawful conscription of government critics.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, the conflict between government forces and allied militias and Islamist armed groups, ongoing since 2017, has involved widespread abuses by all parties, including war crimes and crimes against humanity, with no accountability. Human Rights Watch has documented serious flaws in the special terrorism court, including prolonged pretrial detention, and violations of fair trial guarantees.

    In a recent development, concerned governments should rigorously scrutinize all extradition and judicial cooperation requests from Burkina Faso. No journalist, activist or political opponent should be returned where there are substantial grounds to fear torture, arbitrary detention, an unfair trial, and the death penalty. International partners should condemn the targeting of critics at home and abroad and reject Burkina Faso’s attempts at transnational repression.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that (New York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.

    Recent findings suggest that rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights in 2002, later becoming its president, and co-founded and was executive director of the Gulf Centre for Human Rights starting in 2011.

    Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region.

    Industry observers note that bahraini authorities unjustly detained and imprisoned him several times for his peaceful expression in the years following the 2011 pro-democracy protests in Bahrain. In 2018, he was sentenced to five years in prison for his comments criticizing torture at a Bahraini prison and the Saudi-led military campaign in Yemen. Even from detention, he continued his activism. In 2017, he wrote an op-ed for the New York Times from detention, titled “Don’t Profit from Abuses by Bahrain,” calling out US support of Bahraini authorities despite their abuses both in Bahrain and amid the conflict in Yemen. He wrote:.

    It has been revealed that all our destinies are tied together. What will happen to Bahrain if everyone who supports peace, democracy and the rule of law is in jail? To whom will Bahrain’s disenfranchised youth turn to for support and guidance? These are the questions the Trump administration must ask itself before it sends my jailers another batch of fighter jets.

    Sources indicate that he was released from prison in 2020 and allowed to serve the rest of his sentence at home with his family, but only after his health deteriorated due to harsh detention conditions. In the years that followed, he continued to support the human rights movement and call out human rights abuses by Bahraini and other authorities across the world.

    It has been revealed that sayed Ahmed al-Wadaei, the advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy and a close friend, said that Rajab left Bahrain in March 2026 so that he could speak publicly on Bahraini human rights challenges. He remained in exile until his passing, unable to return to Bahrain for fear of being rearrested.

    Rajab’s death is a profound blow to the global and Arab human rights movements, which have lost a steadfast defender of freedom of expression and a voice of reason in a climate increasingly marked by hatred and polarization. Over many years, Rajab stood resolutely by his principles, despite being targeted, detained, and repressed for his unwavering commitment to universal human rights.

    Industry observers note that “Nabeel was a stalwart champion for human rights and democracy, not just for Bahrain but all of the Middle East,” noted Sarah Leah Whitson, former Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He paid a tremendous price for his advocacy, jailed and abused in prison, but always kept us hopeful and resilient. He played an essential role in guiding and supporting the work of Human Rights Watch’s MENA division. I considered him a true friend.”.

    According to recent reports, “Nabeel’s legacy lives on in the innumerable people he inspired, fought alongside in the defense of rights, and held up, sometimes in their darkest moments,” said Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He has been a leader and guide to human rights defenders in the region. He and his family paid a high price for his activism, but we are grateful for his wisdom, tenacity, and courage.”.

    Industry observers note that nabeel Rajab’s courage, integrity, and principled advocacy will be his enduring legacy. Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and the many friends who mourn his loss.

    Breaking: Sudan: Transfer War Crimes Suspects to ICC

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • On November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him.
    • It has been revealed that “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch stated today. Haroun was recently taken into Sudanese custody and faces ICC war crimes and crimes against humanity charges, committed in Sudan’s Darfur region, in 2003 and 2004.

    On November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him. He was arrested one day after he took part in a video podcast interview, his first public appearance since 2019. The armed forces have not officially confirmed Haroun’s whereabouts, but media reported that he is detained in Khartoum state.

    It has been revealed that “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “If Sudan’s authorities transferred those sought by the ICC to the court in The Hague, as they are obliged to do, it would send a powerful message to those committing crimes today that they too may find themselves in the dock.”.

    Authorities should also transfer former President Omar al-Bashir—who is believed to be in Sudanese custody in Khartoum state as well—and locate, arrest, and transfer former Defense Minister Abdelrahim M. Hussein. The ICC has also issued arrest warrants for both of them, though there is no information available on Hussein’s location.

    The ICC issued an arrest warrant against Haroun in 2007, and another against Hussein in 2012, for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2004. During that period, Sudanese government forces and allied militias carried out targeted attacks against civilians on the basis of their ethnicity, including killings, rape, forced displacement from their homes and land, and burning of their villages. In 2009 and 2010, the ICC issued two arrest warrants against al-Bashir for alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2008.

    Following al-Bashir’s ouster in April 2019, Sudanese authorities held Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein in custody for charges not related to atrocities in Darfur but failed to transfer them to the ICC.

    After fighting erupted between SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023, the authorities moved al-Bashir to Alia military hospital in Omdurman, Khartoum state, where he reportedly remained under guard, while Haroun left detention amid the collapse of prison security, and under circumstances suggesting coordination with judicial authorities.

    Industry observers note that on September 30, 2026, SAF granted al-Bashir initial approval to travel outside of Sudan for medical treatment. Based on media reports, al-Bashir continues to receive medical care at Alia military hospital and is yet to travel abroad.

    UN Security Council Resolution 1593, referring the situation in Darfur to the ICC prosecutor, requires the government of Sudan to cooperate with the court even though it is not a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. In 2021, the ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor signed a memorandum of understanding with the Sudanese authorities addressing cooperation for arrests. The ICC lacks the ability to enforce its own orders and relies on state cooperation to conduct investigations and make arrests.

    It has been revealed that in January and July, the Office of the Prosecutor reported to the United Nations Security Council on its investigation in Darfur, including its continued engagement with Sudanese authorities. In addition to addressing crimes from July 2002 onward, the Office of the Prosecutor is also investigating crimes committed since April 2023 in Darfur. The prosecutor’s office reported “positive” and “significant” cooperation by Sudanese authorities, and assistance in support of its investigative activities, including deployment of the office’s investigative team to Port Sudan.

    Nevertheless, Sudan has not fulfilled its obligation to carry out the court’s arrest warrants and transfer the wanted suspects to the Hague. The authorities should provide public information on the whereabouts of all the wanted suspects and take immediate steps to allow their transfer to the court, Human Rights Watch noted.

    The African Union, the members of the Atrocity Prevention and Justice Coalition for Sudan–– particularly the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Sierra Leone––as well as the European Union and its member states should directly engage with Sudanese authorities, calling on them to comply with their obligation to fully cooperate with the ICC and to transfer Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein to the court’s custody.

    ICC judges have referred to the Security Council several findings of noncooperation against Sudan and ICC member states in relation to the arrest of ICC suspects. However, the council has never taken steps to enforce these findings. UN member states should urge the Security Council to back the ICC’s mandate in Darfur, including by enforcing the court’s findings of noncooperation on arrests.

    The ICC prosecutor’s office should use its next biannual report to the council, in January 2027, as an opportunity to raise any concerns related to Sudan’s cooperation on arrests.

    In 2025, the ICC convicted Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman (also known as Ali Kosheib), a former leader of Sudan’s “Janjaweed” militias, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur in 2003 and 2004, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison. Kosheib’s trial was possible after he surrendered himself voluntarily to the ICC’s custody in 2020.

    Industry observers note that “For victims and survivors of crimes in Darfur, Sudanese authorities’ promises of cooperation mean little without concrete action,” Evenson noted. “Sudan’s international partners should use every diplomatic tool at their disposal to press for the immediate transfer of all ICC suspects in Sudanese custody and make clear that cooperation with the court is not optional.”.

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, from Judge Trina Thompson (N.D.
    • The Court ORDERS that the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages.
    • In a recent development, on July 4, 2025, Secretary [of Agriculture Brooke] Rollins sent an email from her official email account celebrating Independence Day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, from Judge Trina Thompson (N.D. Cal.) today in Nat'l Federation of Federal Employees v. U.S. Dep't of Agriculture:.

    The Court ORDERS that the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages. She "[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [her] to stop," she "[c]annot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances," and she "[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates." USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019. She may "[d]iscuss [her] religious beliefs with interested colleagues," "[s]hare why [her] faith is meaningful to [her]," "[p]olitely invite coworkers to religious services or events," "[e]xpress religious viewpoints during appropriate conversations." This Court expresses no view whatsoever on what the Secretary can and cannot do in her personal capacity….

    In a recent development, on July 4, 2025, Secretary [of Agriculture Brooke] Rollins sent an email from her official email account celebrating Independence Day. The message was sent to all USDA employees. Her message concluded with a written statement, "May God continue to protect the United States of America and may His favor shine over all her land." On November 26, 2025, Rollins sent a Thanksgiving message from her official email account to all USDA employees, attributing the first Thanksgiving in part to "gratitude towards a loving God.".

    The complaint identifies two subsequent communications as expressly promoting Christianity. On December 23, 2025, Rollins emailed USDA employees a Christmas message containing a video in which she stated that "The spirit of generosity flows from the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life. This is the reason for the season….".

    On April 5, 2026, she sent an Easter email addressed to "All USDA Employees" which read:.

    Happy Easter – He is Risen indeed!

    Today we celebrate the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind.

    Recent findings suggest that from the foot of the Cross on Good Friday to the stone rolled away from the now empty tomb, sin has been destroyed. Jesus has been raised from the dead. And God has granted each of us victory and new life. And where there is life — risen life — there is hope.

    Recent findings suggest that no matter the very real trials and hardships we face, fear and sin and death do not get the last word. Because on Easter morning, "Hell took a body, and discovered God. It took earth, and encountered Heaven. It took what it saw, and was overcome by what it did not see." Now that is reason to rejoice!

    And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for.

    In a recent development, please know how amazed and grateful I am for the hard work each of you do to support our shared mission here at USDA. I hope you and your loved ones have a truly blessed and happy Easter. May God continue to bless you, your families, and our exceptional country, One Nation, Under God.

    At the top of the email, Secretary Rollins included an illustration of a stone rolled away from Jesus' tomb with the words "Christ is Risen" written above the illustration.

    In a recent development, plaintiffs allege that Rollins has not sent comparable messages acknowledging other religions' holidays. They contrast her communications with USDA's November 20, 2025 guidance on religious expression, which provides that officials "[c]annot use official authority to pressure subordinates" regarding religious beliefs and "[m]ust stop if a colleague asks [them] to stop." They further allege that Rollins defended the Easter message publicly and is likely to send similar communications marking future Christian holidays.

    Each individual plaintiff received and read the challenged messages. Plaintiffs allege that they are expected to read communications from the Secretary because those communications may contain consequential workplace information. Other messages have addressed agency reorganization, employee relocation, changes to USDA's civil rights program, shutdown planning, and the Deferred Resignation Program; holiday messages have historically included administrative-leave announcements.

    Recent findings suggest that the individual plaintiffs allege that the messages convey a preference for employees who share the Secretary's Christian beliefs, make them feel excluded, and pressure them to conceal their own beliefs or appear to share hers. They fear workplace disfavor and retaliation for objecting; the complaint also alleges that supervisors have warned that objections would result in "trouble." Plaintiff Poopatanapong alleges that she no longer feels safe discussing a Buddhist holiday she celebrates; Roberts, an atheist, feels silenced; and Wolfe, a Pagan, feels pressure to appear Christian to advance professionally. alleges that its USDA members likewise received the messages, felt compelled to read them, and experienced pressure to accept the Secretary's beliefs while withholding their own.

    The court held that plaintiffs' Establishment Clause were likely violated:.

    Sources indicate that the Establishment Clause protects religious freedom by "command[ing] a separation of church and state." Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch. Dist., 597 U.S. 507, 558–59 (2022) (citing Cutter v. Wilkinson, 544 U.S. 709, 719 (2005)). [Note that this quote is actually from Justice Sotomayor's dissent in Kennedy, though it appears in the Cutter majority. -EV] At its core, this means forbidding "sponsorship, financial support, and active involvement of the sovereign in religious activity." As the Supreme Court acknowledged in Kennedy, the Establishment Clause does not "'compel the government to purge from the public sphere' anything an objective observer could reasonably infer endorses or 'partakes of the religious.'" However, courts must be cautious to ensure that "what might begin as a tolerant expression of religious views" does not "end in a policy to indoctrinate and coerce.".

    According to recent reports, to determine whether government action violates the Establishment Clause, the Court must "focus[ ] on original meaning and history" of the First Amendment. That is, this Court's must be guided by "historical practices and understandings" of the relationship between government and religion in America. Pursuant to this approach, any practice that was "accepted by the Framers and has withstood the critical scrutiny of time and political change" does not violate the Establishment Clause. The analysis does not end merely because a practice has been observed in the past. The history and tradition test requires this Court to look to the "uninterrupted practice" of law in our nation's traditions.

    Traditionally, the hallmark of government conduct violative of the Establishment Clause is the presence of some form of coercion upon its citizens.

    Recent findings suggest that thomas Jefferson and James Madison, the two Founders most instrumental in the drafting and ratification of the Religion Clauses of the First Amendment, articulated a founding-era concern broader than direct, compelled sectarian practices. Madison, for example, expressed concern that even instances of governmental "recommendation[]" concerning religion "naturally terminate[] in a conformity to the creed of the majority []." Jefferson expressed concern about indirect forms of coercion such as conduct which might invite "some degree of proscription perhaps in public opinion." Most fitting, in his "Memorial and Remonstrance Against Religious Assessments" drafted in 1785, Madison questioned the ends sought by the promotion of a sectarian underpinning to our country's political foundation: "Who does not see that the same authority which can establish Christianity, in exclusion of all other Religions, may establish with the same ease any particular sect of Christians, in exclusion of all other Sects?" His guidance, contained in the same writings: "Such a Government will be best supported by protecting every Citizen in the enjoyment of his Religion with the same equal hand which protects his person and his property; by neither invading the equal rights of any Sect, nor suffering any Sect to invade those of another." The Founders may have lacked the foresight to account for contemporary technological advances, but the principles embedded in our First Amendment ring as true today. As difficult as the task may be, below, this Court faithfully applies the founding-era's understanding of the Establishment Clause to the modern-day circumstances giving rise to this litigation….

    In a recent development, after reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion. Here, three factors inform the Court's conclusion that the Secretary's conduct was coercive: (1) her position of authority, (2) the use of her official email to send messages to all USDA employees, and (3) the alienating language contained in the emails to employees who did not share her religious tenets. [Detailed discussion of factors 1 and 2 omitted for space reasons. -EV].

    It has been revealed that it makes no difference that the emails did not single out dissidents, disparage those who did not share the Secretary's beliefs, or indicate work-related decisions would be influenced by an employees' reaction to the emails. The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that "immense social pressure" can result in a finding of coercion. Such pressure is demonstrated here…. While social pressure alone is not state coercion because "mature adults … presumably are not readily susceptible to religious indoctrination or peer pressure[,]" the totality of the circumstances here demonstrates such immense pressure to amount to coercion….

    The Court does not purport to regulate the religiosity of the Secretary—nor could it. "A relentless and all-pervasive attempt to exclude religion from every aspect of public life could itself become inconsistent with the Constitution." Nor does this Court generally condemn the expression of religious sentiments. Instead, this Court requires the Secretary to observe her own directives. USDA Secretary's Memorandum 1078-019. The April 5, 2026, and December 23, 2025, messages go too far. They suggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure; a pressure of conformity sufficient to raise an Establishment Clause violation….

    The judge who sentenced British comedian and actor Russell Brand is being given high marks for his sentencing comments, particularly for clarifying rape myths that were presented during the trial.

    High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan sentenced Brand to 10-and-a-half years in prison Monday. In his comments, Bennathan addressed myths surrounding rape and the “enablers” who witnessed Brand’s sexual assaults on women.

    “The judge’s comments are welcome given the significant role that rape myths played in this trial, which in turn have influenced public discussions about the case,” remarked Deniz Uğur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, according to coverage by the Guardian.

    Executives from the Criminal Bar Association of England and Wales noted the “piercing clarity of the judge’s statement.” The judge’s comments were also called “hugely key” because of how high-profile the trial was, according to Ciara Bergman, the CEO of Rape Crisis England & Wales.

    Bergman pointed out that Bennathan’s remarks starkly countered misconceptions presented by the defense attorney, Ian Winter, including that the women should have fought back, screamed or immediately reported the attack.

    “Of course, this is not the case; there are a range of ways in which people respond to the threat of an imminent sexual assault, and all of them are valid,” Bergman mentioned.

    Russell Brand found guilty of rape, sexual assault as judge promises ‘sentence of some length’.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As the International Court of Justice in The Hague delivered its judgment on November 19 in the landmark case that Gambia brought against Myanmar for violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, thousands of Rohingya waited anxiously in refugee camps in Bangladesh.

    In the Jamtoli Camp 15 in Cox's Bazar District, many crowded around a television. About two hours into the reading of the judgment, it started to rain. But no one moved.

    The court’s president spoke in English, a language rarely heard in the crowded camps where over a million Rohingya sought refuge after fleeing Myanmar military attacks in 2017. At 5:13 p.m. local time, a community leader relayed the court’s ruling in the Rohingya language to the waiting crowd, telling them that, by nine votes to six, the court found Myanmar “committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.”.

    The crowd clapped and cheered; many were in tears.

    “The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied,” stated 58-year-old Monajat Alam, from Rathedaung Township. “Today, the truth has been recognized.”.

    Sources indicate that the ruling was based on evidence showing that thousands of Rohingya civilians, including children, had been killed and that there was widespread sexual violence and destruction of villages during the 2017 military campaign. The court found the evidence also indicated that Myanmar intended to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population.

    Industry observers note that nemat Hussen from Maung Nu in Buthidaung Township, where Myanmar soldiers massacred hundreds of Rohingya villagers on August 27, 2017, brought along his son. Maung Nu was one of three villages that Gambia asked the court to examine for evidence of genocidal intent.

    In a recent development, “In 2017, I lost my mother and eldest son,” Maung Nu stated. “Since that day, I’ve been waiting for justice, and today I brought my son to hear the judgment.”.

    The court ordered Myanmar to investigate suspected perpetrators of genocide and prosecute them where warranted, compensate the Rohingya for the harm they suffered, and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of those displaced, among other measures.

    “Today, my hopes have grown tremendously,” Monajat Uddin noted. “I wish that we’ll be able to return to Rakhine and live in peace and our homeland will be safe so that we can return.”.

    #55487. Breaking: Retrospective Voting and the 2026 Election

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1634 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Retrospective Voting and the 2026 Election

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that in my book Democracy and Political Ignorance  and various other writings going all the way back to my very first academic article (published in 1998), I have warned of the dangers of widespread voter ignorance.
    • It has been revealed that retrospective voting is probably the most often-used information shortcut, and the one most cited by scholars who argue that voter ignorance isn't much of a problem.
    • If things are going well, you vote to reelect them to continue their good work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that in my book Democracy and Political Ignorance  and various other writings going all the way back to my very first academic article (published in 1998), I have warned of the dangers of widespread voter ignorance. And I have argued that "information shortcuts" - small bits of knowledge that supposedly make up for ignorance about details - are generally ineffective or even counterproductive. Thus, I should acknowledge that one of those shortcuts - retrospective voting - worked fairly well in the recently concluded 2026 election. At the same time, the problem of political ignorance remains a grave menace.

    It has been revealed that retrospective voting is probably the most often-used information shortcut, and the one most cited by scholars who argue that voter ignorance isn't much of a problem. The basic idea is simple: to be a good voter you don't need to know much about government and public policy. You just need to know whether things are going well or badly under the rule of the incumbents.

    If things are going well, you vote to reelect them to continue their good work. If badly, you vote to "throw the bastards out." Then you elect a upcoming set of bastards in their place; but the new bastards will hopefully know they need to do a good job, else they will get thrown out in their turn, at the next election. As Ronald Reagan famously put it during the 1980 election, "Next Tuesday all of you will go to the polls… I think when you make that decision it might be well if you would ask yourself: Are you better off than you were four years ago?".

    I and other critics have long pointed out that, when ignorant voters use the retrospective voting shortcut, they often end up rewarding and punishing incumbents for things they did not cause (usually short-term economic trends), while ignoring more subtle long-term issues. In addition, they often don't know which officials are responsible for which issues, and tend to overlook the possibility that the opposition party's policies will be as bad or worse.

    According to recent reports, nonetheless, retrospective voting actually worked pretty well in the 2026 election. As I noted in a previous post, polls show that many voters punished the Republicans for high prices caused by Trump's tariffs,  the failed Iran War, and the administration's cruel campaign of mass deportations (which particularly angered Hispanic voters in key states and congressional districts). One can also add the problem of corruption, which polls  indicate also had a substantial impact.

    The Republicans really were responsible for all three of these policies. They weren't caused by exogenous factors outside of Trump's control. And the policies really did have massive negative effects in raising prices, an unsuccessful war, and massive cruelty and violations of civil liberties caused by the deportation campaign. The scope and effects of corruption are harder to measure. But this administration may be the most corrupt in American history. And, on all four challenges, the Democrats are likely to be at least somewhat better.

    But while retrospective voting worked reasonably well in the 2026 midterm election, we cannot conclude that the problem of political ignorance doesn't matter, or even that it's overblown. Rather, the shortcut was effective primarily because of the large and obvious nature of Trump's failures.

    Recent findings suggest that along with other scholars, I have long recognized that retrospective voting can be effective if incumbents screw in ways that have large and obvious bad effects - ones that even very ignorant voters can easily see and understand. For example, I often cite economist Amartya Sen's famous finding that mass famines never or almost never occur under democracies (even as they happen much more often under dictatorships). Even ignorant voters will notice a famine is going on, blame incumbents for it, and vote accordingly.

    Recent findings suggest that trump's failures over the last two years weren't quite as bad as a mass famine. But they were nonetheless large (including a major war and  the highest tariff schedule since the Great Depression), highly visible, and many of their effects were easy to understand. It isn't hard to notice that massive tariff increases cause prices to rise. The war and its effects on prices were also highly visible. Images of brutal deportations and resulting civil liberties violations were all over the news. Most voters probably didn't know about the details of the administration's corruption. But there was so much of it, that most probably heard at least something about it.

    Industry observers note that many policy failures are far less readily apparent than that. And ignorant voters are therefore likely to overlook or misunderstand them. It's not hard to find examples even in the 2026 election itself. To take a particularly important case, the US faces a massive looming fiscal crisis, caused in large part by the combination of an aging population and out-of-control entitlement spending. Yet most candidates of both parties largely ignored this problem, and promise continued massive spending, and avoiding tax increases for almost everyone, except perhaps a few billionaires and other very wealthy people. They could do that because surveys show most voters are ignorant about our fiscal situation and especially don't realize the key role of entitlement spending.

    Voters' justified negative reaction in 2026 to tariffs, mass deportations, corruption, and the Iran War also highlight the failure of information shortcuts in the 2024 election. At that time, it was evident to informed observers that Trump would seek to institute massive tariffs and cruel deportation policies. Indeed, I myself was among those who cited them as among the principal reasons to oppose Trump in that election. Large-scale corruption was also predictable, given Trump's long history of skullduggery. Yet swing voters got these challenges wrong - despite the fact that high prices were a major issue in 2024, and tariffs and mass deportations would predictably raise them (as I also pointed out at the time).

    Recent findings suggest that the Iran War was admittedly less predictable. Trump even promised to avoid new wars. But his well-documented combination of ignorance and impulsiveness meant that returning him to office created a significant risk of a foreign policy crisis spiraling out of control.

    It has been revealed that and on all these issues, it was predictable (and predicted by many, including me) that Trump 2.0 would surround himself with cronies and loyalists likely to indulge his worst instincts. No longer would he be constrained by "adults in the room," as occasionally happened during his first term.

    Sources indicate that thus, while an information shortcut worked well in 2026, it's important to recognize that was only necessary because shortcuts failed miserably in 2024, which was an only modestly more difficult situation. In that earlier election, we did not yet see the effects of Trump's awful second-term policies. But most of those policies and effects were readily predictable by any moderately well-informed observer. Yet most swing voters were much more ignorant than that, and thus instead voted to punish Democrats for high prices, ignoring the high likelihood that electing Trump would make that problem worse, not better.

    In addition, as I emphasized in my November 2024 post on voter ignorance in that year's election, a combination of ignorance and bias led many voters to underestimate the significance of Trump's assault on basic norms and principles of liberal democracy.

    It has been revealed that it is also crucial to remember that the problem of voter ignorance is not just that it leads voters to make "wrong" choices between the options put before them. It also makes those options worse in the first place. As I have long argued in my book and elsewhere, political ignorance also makes those options worse in the first place. Politicians and campaign strategists know they face a largely ignorant electorate, and act accordingly. Sweeping the fiscal crisis under the rug is just one of many examples of that tendency. Even if information shortcuts consistently helped voters choose the lesser of the evils before them (which, sadly, they don't!), ignorance would still make those options much more evil than they would be otherwise.

    Trump is a particularly egregious long-time exploiter of political ignorance, which played key roles in his rise and return to power. But more conventional politicians also routinely exploit it, as Barack Obama did, for example. For those keeping score, I have been arguing that political ignorance is a serious danger for over 25 years, under both Republican and Democratic administrations, and through many changes in the political winds.

    The  2024 election led me to conclude that voter ignorance was an even more serious problem than I previously thought. This year's election is, perhaps, a data point for the other side. But whether or not the problem is worse than I thought before 2024, it continues to be a serious danger.

    Sources indicate that there is no easy fix for widespread voter ignorance. I assessed  various possible options in my 2023 book chapter on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in Chapters 5-7 of Democracy and Political Ignorance. I think the most promising approach make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and use it wisely are better. I also argue in both works that the idea of simply paying voters to increase their knowledge deserves more attention. But any remedy will take time, and we may need a combination of several strategies, not just one.

    In sum, the 2026 election is an example of retrospective voting working relatively well. But we should not conclude this shortcut - or any other - is a good general solution to the problem of widespread political ignorance.

    • (The Hague) – The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • Sources indicate that in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention), the court ruled for Gambia, with a nine to six vote by the judges, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.
    • It has been revealed that “The landmark International Court of Justice ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” remarked Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (The Hague) – The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice, Human Rights Watch said today. On November 19, 2026, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations,” carried out by Myanmar’s military.

    Sources indicate that in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention), the court ruled for Gambia, with a nine to six vote by the judges, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. This is the first time that the ICJ found a country responsible for committing genocide. The court also found that Myanmar violated other obligations under the Genocide Convention, including the obligations to punish those responsible for genocide and to prevent genocide. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

    It has been revealed that “The landmark International Court of Justice ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” remarked Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide and other grave crimes across the world in their own search for justice.”.

    Industry observers note that in August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the ICJ alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention. This was also the first time that a country without any direct connection to the alleged crimes used its membership in the Genocide Convention to bring a case before the ICJ.

    Recent findings suggest that the ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, adjudicating disputes between states and issuing advisory opinions on international law. It consists of 15 judges elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council for nine-year terms.

    In its ruling, the ICJ found that the evidence before it established that Myanmar’s security forces, and other state organs, intentionally committed the genocidal acts of killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births against the Rohingya.

    Considering the totality of the evidence, the court concluded that Myanmar committed these acts with the requisite genocidal intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population of Myanmar. To reach this conclusion, it considered an array of relevant factors, including the general context, the selective targeting of the Rohingya, acts that violated the foundations of the Rohingya group, such as sexual violence and targeting children, and the systematic nature of Myanmar’s actions.

    Based on these factors, the court found that Myanmar’s genocidal intent was “the only reasonable inference” that could be drawn from the evidence before it. The judges rejected the possibility that other alternative intents, such as to carry out counterinsurgency operations or to forcibly displace the Rohingya, could reasonably explain Myanmar’s conduct.

    In light of its findings, the court ordered Myanmar to cease its ongoing violations of the Genocide Convention, including its failure to enact legislation to give effect to the convention and its failure to investigate, prosecute, and punish genocide. It found that Myanmar needs to provide assurances of non-repetition and is obliged to prevent similar violations in the future.

    According to recent reports, the court also established that Gambia was entitled to seek reparations on behalf of Rohingya victims and ordered Myanmar to provide them. These include forms of restitution such as allowing and facilitating the safe, voluntary and dignified return of the Rohingya to their place of residence, and the reunification of displaced families. Whenever restitution is materially impossible, the court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations in the form of compensation.

    According to recent reports, the court’s reasoning in this case is expected to have a profound impact on other pending cases before the ICJ regarding alleged violations of the Genocide Convention. This includes the case filed by South Africa against Israel in December 2023.

    Industry observers note that prior to the Myanmar judgment, US officials sought to pressure the ICJ and its judges with regard to the legal threshold for genocide. The US government has already sanctioned the International Criminal Court and several of its officials in an effort to shield senior US and Israeli officials from facing serious crimes charges before the court.

    Recent findings suggest that in February 2021, following the November 2020 Myanmar elections won by Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy, the then-commander-in-chief, Sr. Gen. Min Aung Hlaing, led a military coup that overthrew the civilian government. More than five years later, Myanmar’s military junta continues to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity throughout the country. Min Aung Hlaing installed himself as president through fraudulent elections in December 2025 and January 2026.

    In Rakhine State since late 2023, Rohingya civilians have been caught in the hostilities between the junta and ethnic Arakan Army forces. Both parties have carried out grave abuses, including extrajudicial killings, widespread arson, and unlawful recruitment. The Myanmar military continues to commit war crimes against the Rohingya and the crimes against humanity of apartheid, persecution, and deprivation of liberty. The Arakan Army, which now controls most of Rakhine State, has tightened repression of the Rohingya, including forced labor and arbitrary detention, and has committed grave violations of the laws of war amounting to war crimes.

    ICJ judgments are legally binding on the parties to the case. If one party considers that the other has failed to comply with the court’s ruling, it may turn to the Security Council, which can “make recommendations or decide upon measures to be taken to give effect to the judgment.” The Security Council has never acted upon this discretionary power.

    The UN General Assembly can galvanize political support to enforce ICJ judgments by adopting resolutions calling for compliance. Individual countries can also influence compliance through their bilateral engagement with the relevant party.

    Eleven countries that are parties to the Genocide Convention intervened in Gambia’s case on limited concerns relating to the construction of the convention. The court’s interpretation of the convention on these issues becomes legally binding for them.

    The ICJ ruling is a clear reminder of the importance of independent judicial institutions in upholding international law, Human Rights Watch remarked.

    Sources indicate that “Myanmar should swiftly comply with the World court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya,” Vignoli remarked. “Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.”.
