    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • Recent findings suggest that container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of.
    • Industry observers note that your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth. More than 9 million developers and 250,000+ customers now build on Supabase, and the majority of new databases on the platform are created by AI app builders — so the systems underneath have to stay reliable while they grow fast.

    Recent findings suggest that container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of. We own cluster lifecycle and cluster classes, multi-cluster and multi-region topology, capacity, scheduling, isolation and runtime safety, the higher-level platform APIs, the Kubernetes deployment contract and Argo semantics, rollout primitives, and runtime configuration and secret injection.

    Industry observers note that your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it. This is not a gatekeeper role. You'll make the reliable path the easy path: building the automation and platform APIs that let product teams run safely by default, instrumenting what we operate, and making sure that when something breaks we detect it and recover fast.

    The work spans three strength areas:.

    Tooling & ecosystem — deep knowledge of the container and orchestration landscape (Kubernetes, containerd/OCI, the CNCF ecosystem) and a clear point of view on how to compose it.

    Software engineering — designing and building the platform's automation, controllers, and internal tooling as production code, including solutions that don't come pre-shaped by an existing tool.

    Operational / SRE practice — the discipline (SLOs, error budgets, incident response, ORRs) that runs the platform at scale as a predictable one.

    We expect you to be genuinely deep in at least one of these, and many of our strongest candidates are deep in two (usually leaning toward one). Bringing real strength across all three is rare and exceptional — and even then, no one is equally strong in all three at once, so you'd focus where you're most needed at any given time. Different profiles are welcome here; tell us which of these is your center of gravity.

    Regardless of the skill set, all team members carry a share of the team's on-call rota, responding to platform incidents and driving them to resolution and follow-up.

    Platform reliability & operations.

    Define SLIs/SLOs and error budgets for the container platform itself, and build error-budget policies that actually gate platform changes.

    Own the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process for latest platform capabilities and major changes.

    Design and track metrics for platform uptime, and increase observability into the platform by capturing the right metrics, logs, and traces across the platform layers.

    Drive the incident-to-improvement pipeline: facilitate blameless postmortems, connect findings to readiness gaps, spot repeat failure patterns, and push through systemic fixes.

    Build and maintain the platform's automation, controllers, operators, and internal tooling — writing production code and shipping it, not just wiring together existing tools.

    Design and implement the platform-side CI/CD and rollout primitives that speed up platform deployments while working within proper change and release management.

    Implement and maintain security automation for the platform: intrusion detection, automated remediation, and patch management.

    Identify and quantify operational toil, and build the automation that removes it rather than just documenting it.

    Contribute to the platform's continual testing automation — the test suites and pipelines that validate platform releases are fit for purpose before they reach tenants.

    Tooling, ecosystem & architecture.

    Act as a platform reliability and architecture expert — contribute to failure-mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design for multi-tenant container workloads.

    Evaluate and evolve the platform's tooling ecosystem (orchestration, runtime, networking, isolation, and observability stack) with a clear, opinionated view on trade-offs.

    Improve system architecture to reduce infrastructure cost while balancing security, reliability, and performance across tenants.

    Guide teams building on the platform to design sustainable on-call practices for their own services: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction.

    Have 5+ years in platform engineering, container/Kubernetes platform operations, SRE, or production infrastructure, and have operated production systems at scale and carried on-call for them.

    Are genuinely deep in at least one — ideally two — of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):.

    According to recent reports, tooling & ecosystem — know the container/orchestration landscape well: Kubernetes, containerd and the OCI/CRI standards, and the surrounding CNCF ecosystem (e.g. Argo CD/Argo Rollouts for GitOps and progressive delivery; Cilium/eBPF networking and the Gateway API; Karpenter/KEDA-style autoscaling; and workload-isolation runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers). You reason about trade-offs rather than reaching for defaults.

    Software engineering — write real production code (Go and/or a comparable systems language) and can build controllers, operators, and platform APIs — stepping back to the underlying problem and building the right solution when no off-the-shelf tool fits.

    Operational / SRE practice — are fluent in SLOs, error budgets, and operational KPIs; have led incident response and blameless postmortems; and have driven down MTTD/MTTR for systems you operated.

    Have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems and understand isolation as a spectrum — from namespaces, RBAC, network policies, and resource quotas through to stronger primitives such as virtual clusters (e.g. vCluster) or VM-class runtimes.

    Operate confidently on AWS (multiple accounts, IAM, VPC) and are comfortable with infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred; Terraform/CDK also fine) and Kubernetes.

    Script and automate to eliminate toil rather than absorb it.

    Communicate clearly with both infrastructure specialists and product engineers, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and iterating toward better systems over time.

    Experience building and operating a multi-tenant Kubernetes platform that internal teams deploy onto.

    Familiarity with policy engines (Kyverno, or OPA/Gatekeeper) and cost-attribution tooling (OpenCost/Kubecost) for per-tenant chargeback/showback.

    Experience with managed database platforms or Postgres.

    Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Industry observers note that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    Sources indicate that once a year, the entire company gathers in a newly introduced city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Industry observers note that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #55483. 7 mysteries that focus on the motive behind crimes

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1203 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    7 mysteries that focus on the motive behind crimes

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that means, motive, opportunity: they comprise the classic triad of mystery fiction.
    • It has been revealed that for two decades before I wrote my debut novel, On the Killer’s Trail, I worked in education and libraries.
    • Here are seven novels that focus on motive in a variety of ways.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that means, motive, opportunity: they comprise the classic triad of mystery fiction. Of the three features, I appreciate motive as the real heart of a mystery story.

    It has been revealed that for two decades before I wrote my debut novel, On the Killer’s Trail, I worked in education and libraries. Prior to that, I was a psychology major and a social worker. I have always been fascinated by what makes people tick. While the success of a work of fiction in any genre may depend on the specifics, for me, its true value lies in the universal truths about human experience that it portrays and reveals. In Louise Penny’s words, “crime was deeply human.”.

    Here are seven novels that focus on motive in a variety of ways.

    Agatha Christie, Five Little Pigs.

    Sources indicate that no one weaves a mystery from its three strands better than the grande dame of crime fiction, Agatha Christie. In Five Little Pigs, a young woman asks Hercule Poirot to investigate the death of her father for which her mother was convicted sixteen years earlier. The evidence at trial was overwhelming and the accused woman’s defense weak.

    Shortly before her own death, the mother professed her innocence to her child in a letter. Due to the passage of time, Poirot must depend on character, rather than evidence, to solve the case. He says, “[Character] is the principal interest of all my cases.” The “five little pigs” are the five people, other than the wife, who had the opportunity to kill Amyas Crane, a talented but eminently unlikeable painter.

    In a recent development, initially, none of the five appears to have a motive to murder him. Poirot tells one of the suspects, “the reason for murder is nearly always to be found by a study of the person murdered.” As Poirot delves into the past, he uncovers the truth about Crane’s life and learns that each of the five did, indeed, have a motive. His analysis of the behavior and motivations of several of the suspects ultimately leads him to the solution.

    More than sixty years after Christie’s novel was published, Louise Penny introduces another wise Francophone inspector, Armande Gamache. He, too, investigates the murder of an artist.

    In a recent development, the puzzle in Still Life is that, unlike Christie’s victim, Jane Neal of the idyllic Quebecois village of Three Pines was beloved by all. When Neal’s body is found in the woods, felled by an arrow, on Thanksgiving morning, Gamage asks, “who would want to kill kindness?” He later explains “most premeditated murders were about rancid emotions, greed, jealousy, fear, all repressed.”.

    Penny introduces us to a host of Three Pines villagers, among whom are both suspects and others who will become fond recurring characters in future books, the twenty-first of which was just published this fall.

    Heather Young, The Distant Dead.

    Sal, a lonely sixth-grade boy, discovers the burned body of middle-school teacher Adam Merkel in the Nevada desert. Merkel had befriended the traumatized boy who came to live on a nearby ranch with his reclusive uncles after the death of his mother.

    Recent findings suggest that when one of Adam’s colleagues, who is dealing with her own personal challenges, takes it upon herself to investigate, she uncovers secrets in Adam’s past as she also senses that Sal knows more about Adam’s death than he will admit. Her consideration of possible motives explores how the past and present are immutably intertwined.

    Celeste Ng, Everything I Never Told You.

    Sources indicate that sixteen-year-old Lydia Lee has gone missing. When her body is found in a local lake, her devastated parents need to know how and why it happened. Was it a drowning accident, suicide, or foul play?

    According to recent reports, while this moving novel is not a mystery in the traditional sense, it is an exquisite portrayal of how we are shaped by our families and our experiences and how our motives and actions arise from them. As the family’s emotions and secrets long held in silence are slowly and painfully brought to light, we learn the secrets that Lydia, her siblings, her parents, and their parents have harbored, which ultimately reveal Lydia’s fate.

    Industry observers note that this historical legal mystery is set in a small town in 1946 Mississippi. Pete Banning is an upright, church-going model citizen and World War II hero. After returning from the Philippines and the horrors of his war experience there, he hopes to resume the life he left behind with his wife Liza and their children on their cotton farm. When he has Liza committed to a psychiatric hospital and, soon after, calmly shoots his pastor and friend, Dexter Belland, Banning refuses to defend himself, stating only, “I have nothing to say.”.

    Inspired by an actual case from the 1930’s in which the defendant made the same statement until his execution, Grisham keeps the reader guessing until the end why Banning is prepared to die, rather than reveal his motive.

    Anthony Horowitz, The Magpie Murders.

    A murder mystery within a murder mystery. Editor Susan Ryeland receives the manuscript of her client, author Alan Conway’s latest mystery novel featuring detective Atticus Pund, but with the story’s ending missing.

    It has been revealed that when Conway is found dead, Ryeland concludes that the manuscript involves real-life events and that Conway’s murderer stole the final pages to avoid incrimination. Ryeland sets out to find the motive and perpetrator of Pund’s fictional mystery to find Conway’s real-life killer.

    Stuart Turton, The 7 ½ Deaths of Evelyn Hardcastle.

    Straddling genres, this mystery borrows from speculative fiction to shift time and perspective as the protagonist investigates a murder from the viewpoints of multiple characters within the setting of a classic English country estate. Aiden Bishop wakes up at Blackheath Manor with amnesia and no knowledge of why he is there.

    Recent findings suggest that in each of eight days in a time loop, he finds himself inhabiting a different guest at the manor until he can solve the murder of the young heiress of the estate, Evelyn Hardcastle, who died that evening. If he cannot solve the case by the end of day eight, he is doomed to repeat the cycle with his memory wiped clean.

    Recent findings suggest that whatever the setting or sub-genre, the key to a murder mystery is motive. As Inspector Armande Gamage put it, “My job is to find people who take lives. And to do that, I have to find out why.”.

    Alice Openshaw has been a fan of mysteries since the age of ten, when she discovered Perry Mason books at her tiny town’s public library. She holds a BA in psychology from Middlebury College in Vermont and an MLS from Vanderbilt University. She lived in rural Maine for thirty years, where she worked as a librarian and adult literacy teacher and raised three children and an assortment of animals on a small farm. She now lives near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, with her husband and her tuxedo cat, Frankie. On the Killer's Trail is her debut novel.

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1127 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Catherine Townsend on treating dating like detective work, and vice versa

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that when I was a dating columnist for The Independent in London, I would often point out the similarities between dating and detective work.
    • Conducting investigative interviews is, in crucial ways, very much like being on one long and strange first date.
    • A more cynical take would be that falling in love is like one long con.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that when I was a dating columnist for The Independent in London, I would often point out the similarities between dating and detective work. I’d flag that in both scenarios, you find yourself sitting in front of a stranger—the difference being that in a potential love match, the skeletons in their closet are (hopefully) merely metaphorical, rather than decomposing in a crawl space.

    The same logic works in reverse. Conducting investigative interviews is, in crucial ways, very much like being on one long and strange first date. The idea is to ask open-ended questions and to encourage the person you are trying to get information from to keep talking about themselves. If they keep talking, eventually you can find the inconsistencies in their story.

    A more cynical take would be that falling in love is like one long con. When we like someone, our brain is wired to look for commonalities. And the more we like someone, the more we mimic their behavior. This works extremely well for getting someone to trust you— and that is why con artists mimic our movements, too, for less pure reasons.

    But my job when I’m conducting an interview is to see the worst in people.

    In a recent development, in 2010, I was living in Los Angeles, had just enrolled in PI school with Dale, and was moonlighting as a PI. State boards give credit to-ward investigative hours for police work, which is why retired police detectives can qualify as licensed private investigators. But, despite the fact that investigative journalism uses a lot of the same skill sets as detective work, journalists are given zero credit for hours worked in newsrooms.

    According to recent reports, my first encounters with law enforcement had been less than satisfactory, and I was convinced that this was because, for the most part, they didn’t trust the media. So I wanted to get some more specialized training, something that would raise my skill levels and, hopefully, my esteem in the eyes of the police departments that I was trying to sweet-talk.

    Living in Los Angeles, the quintessential sunny place for shady people, is like having permanent residence inside a noir mystery painted with the rainbow neon sunsets, and traffic jams, of Grand Theft Auto V.

    Dale sent me out on a lot of matrimonial surveillances, and they almost always unfolded in the same way.

    Sometimes, the clients would summon me to their homes. But, following the detective manual logic on interrogations, I preferred to coax the clients into nonthreatening, neutral territory—preferably one that invoked feelings of nostalgia. I found that magic location sliding into a red leatherette booth at Bob’s Big Boy diner in Burbank at sunrise, sipping a ten-ounce mug of Big Boy medium roast, and watching the pink clouds float across an impossibly bright, Monet-meets-vaporwave California sky.

    After that, things usually get complicated. The client asks me to follow their boyfriend/husband/girlfriend/married boyfriend who also has another girlfriend but has promised that they are his only mistress. (I pretend to ignore the logical fallacies of that argument.) I ask them what they hope to accomplish from a surveillance.

    It has been revealed that I’m honest: I’ll tell them that it’s expensive, uncertain, and a hell of a lot harder than it looks on TV. (If you don’t believe me, try identifying a subject described as “white man in a suit” outside a downtown office building at night from a fuzzy Facebook photo. Bonus points if it’s a rainy winter night and only a few inches of skin are visible!).

    I’ll also ask them why they believe that their loved one has been unfaithful, and often they will tell me something that lets me know that they already know the truth: Maybe they have found a topless selfie of his secretary, or a scrap of lacy women’s underwear in the glove compartment of his Prius.

    It has been revealed that I try to always have these conversations over something sweet, which is why I prefer to meet at restaurants. I load the table with strawberry waffles or a banana milkshake with extra maraschino cherries, since bad news goes down easier with a heavy dose of sugar lubricant. Even Cinnabon at the mall food court is better than nothing: Studies show that our animal brains associate the smells of cinnamon and vanilla with comfort and security.

    Industry observers note that “Well, it sounds like you already know the answer,” I inevitably say. Why would you think that this is a good person, despite mounting evidence to the contrary?

    In a recent development, before I dig in and disrupt lives, potentially unearthing a truth that could shake the foundations of a person’s existence, I always ask the same question: Do you really want to know? Little white lies can be the glue that holds relationships together. No, you don’t look fat in those white jeans. Yes, you’re the best sex I’ve ever had.

    I make a point of sliding one of my Patrick Bateman-style thick business cards across the table and making a reference to The Matrix: Would they rather take the blue pill and remain blissfully ignorant, or the red pill to see where the rabbit hole, however unpleasant, leads?

    Industry observers note that some people have a compulsive need to know the reality, however brutal and disruptive it will be to their existence, and they will continue to pick it apart like an overeager esthetician digging out blackheads on YouTube. And then there are those who decide that for whatever reason—long marriage, double mortgage, social hierarchy, or something else—they want to stay inside the much happier bubble they have created.

    Before you ask a question that could shatter your reality forever, it’s important to know which camp you fall into. Because once the bubble is pierced, it’s almost impossible to get back in—and if a person chooses to overlook a betrayal, an infidelity, or something worse, lying to themselves afterward can become a full-time job.

    In a recent development, catherine Townsend is a journalist, private investigator, and podcaster. She is the host of the iHeartMedia podcast Hell and Gone and Red Collar. After beginning her career as a staff writer for Newly introduced York Magazine, Catherine moved to London to create The Independent’s very popular “Sleeping Around” dating column. Her articles have appeared in publications including The Atlantic, Elle, New York, GQ, Marie Claire, Cosmopolitan, The Daily Mail, The New York Post, Investigation Discovery, and HuffPost. She became a licensed private investigator in 2013. She is the author of How to Survive a Murder Investigation: A True Story of Death and Danger in the Ozarks.

    A New York attorney was sentenced Thursday to eight months in prison for embezzling over $500,000 from a trust that he oversaw, according to the Connecticut U.S. attorney’s office.

    According to recent reports, edward W. Miller, 71, of Lawrence, New York, was sentenced to prison by U.S. District Judge Sarala V. Nagala in Hartford, Connecticut.

    David X. Sullivan, the U.S. attorney for the District of Connecticut, announced the sentence after Miller was found guilty of stealing more than $500,000 from a property trust that he managed from February 2016 to September 2022, owned by a person identified as “M.P.” in court records.

    Miller used his position as a trustee to write and negotiate unauthorized checks that he then made payable to himself, his law practice and family members, according to prosecutors and coverage by Law360.

    Miller pleaded guilty to wire fraud earlier this year and said he refinanced his home to pay back the trust. Miller made full restitution of $509,372.82, part of a settlement of a separate civil lawsuit filed by the victims.

    In addition to eight months in prison, Miller was also sentenced to one year of supervised release.

    #55478. Cutting the deadwood with Clive Cussler – my Dad

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1068 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Cutting the deadwood with Clive Cussler – my Dad

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that when the opportunity arose to co-write with Clive Cussler, I thought it would be a uniquely fun experience.
    • According to recent reports, I knew Clive as a genial, good-natured man who loved a good laugh.
    • And so it was– until I submitted an early chapter in our first book together.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that when the opportunity arose to co-write with Clive Cussler, I thought it would be a uniquely fun experience. After all, he was my father.

    According to recent reports, I knew Clive as a genial, good-natured man who loved a good laugh. He was the type of person who expected a lot from himself, but not from others. Growing up, I had ducked household chores as a kid, crashed the family car as a teen, and frittered away college tuition money on pizza and beer, all without incurring any lasting parental disdain. I expected our collaboration on adventure stories to be equally lighthearted and unruffled.

    And so it was– until I submitted an early chapter in our first book together. I had written a scene in which our protagonist, Dirk Pitt, was beaten to a bloody pulp by a nefarious villain. I had crossed a line with Clive’s protagonist, and the curtain of joviality suddenly came crashing down. It was then and there that I realized the man who didn’t take life at all seriously was dead serious about his writing. Clive knew exactly how he wanted his adventure stories crafted, and he was uncompromising about their execution.

    Sources indicate that it took me back to when I was six years old, and my father began writing at night and on weekends in my childhood bedroom, which also served as the family den. He had stacks of paperback books on his desk by the likes of Hammond Innes, Donald Hamilton, and Alistair MacLean. Key passages and sections of dialogue were carefully underlined as he studied the contemporary masters of adventure writing like a Rhodes scholar.

    According to recent reports, clive brought that same dedication to research into his own stories. He loved history, and early on began incorporating historical hooks as key elements in his books. But he never made these inclusions lightly; they were always thoroughly researched.

    In the prologue to Treasure, a Roman legion is attacked by frontier barbarians in 391 A.D. The legionnaires are supported by an historically accurate contingent of Syrian archers and armed with laminated oval shields unique to that particular era of fading Roman dominance. His descriptions of the weaponry, military organization, and battle tactics demonstrated an impressive depth of study.

    In a recent development, I was a young teen when Clive wrote his breakout bestseller, Raise the Titanic! He threw himself into researching the Titanic, borrowing every library book he could find on the ship. He joined the Titanic Historical Society to obtain its quarterly journals and enlisted me to stay up with him to watch the British production of A Night to Remember on late-night television. Such was his devotion to the topic that when he purchased and built a Revell plastic model of the ship, he manually extended the lengths of the funnels when he discovered they weren’t properly to scale. The joy he took in his research was reflected in his fictional raising of the grand ship and having it complete its maiden voyage to Fresh York.

    I share his passion for research, finding it one of the more rewarding aspects of writing. We often discussed the delicate balance involved in incorporating detailed research into a story. Knowledge of the fine details and nuances of a subject can add great flavor to a scene, but there’s also a risk of information overload. As writers, we become mini-experts on a topic and feel compelled to share our newfound knowledge. One common pitfall involves describing places we’ve visited. A writer on vacation in Dublin might later incorporate a night at a pub into a chapter scene. Eager to share the experience, she spends two pages describing the weathered wooden floor, the dusty bottles of whiskey lined above the bar, and the clover designs of the cardboard drink coasters on the tables. An atmospheric plunge suddenly turns into a boring travelogue.

    Those of us who co-wrote with Clive were more than familiar with the crossed-out manuscript pages he would return to us when we got carried away with our own exuberant descriptions.

    Industry observers note that “Cut out the deadwood,” he would implore. “Make it fly.”.

    Recent findings suggest that clive always wanted to drive the narrative forward, but he wasn’t averse to expounding in detail at notable points in the story. He might explain an ancient mystery in depth, such as the history of Troy and its related archaeological excavations in Trojan Odyssey. Or he might dive deep into describing an advanced technology incorporated into the story. These passages weren’t intended to demonstrate his knowledge, but to educate readers about elements that ultimately mattered to the plot.

    Clive was a product of his time, and that also influenced his outlook on pacing and structure. Going to the movies was a ritual in his childhood, and he religiously attended matinees every Saturday afternoon. The main features were preceded by short movie serials, such as The Hurricane Express, which starred a young John Wayne. I know this because a local Denver television station aired the episodes in the 1970s, and my father watched them every week with a bowl of popcorn, as if he were eight years old again. Each episode was less than twenty minutes long, requiring a quick setup, an action sequence or two, and, of course, an ending cliffhanger. He wrote with that same sort of pacing and visual storytelling in mind. Clive especially relished ending a chapter with a cliffhanger, keeping readers eager to turn the page.

    Ultimately, it was the swashbuckling sense of fun those films imparted that most influenced his approach to writing. He was more interested in entertaining readers than impressing them with his prose, and entertainment always took precedence. Clive wanted his stories to be gripping and fast-paced, of course, but the key ingredient may have been the very quality that defined his own character: a genuine sense of fun.

    Dirk Cussler is the author of Clive Cussler's The Devil's Sea, and coauthor with Clive Cussler of eight previous Dirk Pitt adventures: Black Wind, Treasure of Khan, Arctic Drift, Crescent Dawn, Poseidon's Arrow, Havana Storm, Odessa Sea, and Celtic Empire. He serves as president of NUMA, where he continues his father's legacy of searching for crucial historical shipwrecks. He lives in Connecticut.

    #55477. Elly Griffiths’ 5 favorite female detectives in fiction

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1116 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Elly Griffiths’ 5 favorite female detectives in fiction

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, women have always solved crimes.
    • It was some time, though, before crime-solving women appeared in print.
    • Interestingly, these first women sleuths were professionals, in that they earned their living from detection.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, women have always solved crimes. I’m sure Eve knew immediately who killed Abel, although admittedly there was only one suspect. Grendel’s mother, in Beowulf, is one of the greatest justice-seekers in literature. The Wife of Bath would make a formidable sleuth, specializing in domestic cases.

    It was some time, though, before crime-solving women appeared in print. In The Female Detective by Andrew Forrester (the pseudonym of James Redding Ware), published in 1864, Mrs Gladden is thought to be a dressmaker but is, in fact, a detective. The Revelations of a Lady Detective by William Hayward, also published in 1864, features Mrs Paschall, recruited by the Chief of Police to form a squad of women officers. In Mr Bazalgette’s Agent by Leonard Merrick, published in 1888, Miriam Lea is an aristocrat who becomes a private eye after falling on hard times.

    Interestingly, these first women sleuths were professionals, in that they earned their living from detection. The era of the talented but overlooked amateur, exemplified by Miss Marple, comes later.

    Sources indicate that when I created forensic archaeologist Dr Ruth Galloway, I was drawing on the tradition of the civilian expert, often a woman, who assists the police. There many great unofficial detectives in modern crime fiction;  Freida Klein in Nicki French’s books, for example, or Rhona Macleod in Lin Anderson’s series. There are also many terrific women police officers: Val McDermid’s Karen Pirie, Sarah Hilary’s Marnie Rome, Nadine Matheson’s Anjelica Henley,  Jane Casey’s Maeve Kerrigan.

    Here are five of my favorite female detectives, official or otherwise.

    She’s not, strictly speaking, a detective but Marian Halcombe in The Woman in White by Wilkie Collins, is surely one of the greatest sleuths in crime fiction. Laura Fairlie is ostensibly the heroine but Marian, clever, brave and intrepid, is the beating heart of the book.

    The Woman in White, published in 1859/60, is known as one of the great “sensation novels” and the sweeping narrative includes abduction, organized crime and murder. One of the most thrilling scenes has Marian clambering over rooftops at night in order to overhear a conversation between the villains Percival Glyde and Count Fosco. She’s in her petticoat because her voluminous silk skirt would have rustled too much. No wonder even evil Fosco is more than half in love with her.

    No list would be complete without Agatha Christie’s famous spinster sleuth. Jane Marple was apparently inspired by the many unmarried women after the first world war, who, as they grew older, were often ignored by the world around them.

    According to recent reports, miss Marple, poised with rose clippers in her garden or bent over her crochet, makes the most of her invisibility. Almost every crime reminds Miss Marple of something she saw in her home village of St Mary Mead. She’s caustic, quietly brilliant and ruthless when on the trail of a murderer. In A Caribbean Mystery Jason Rafiel describes her as “Nemesis in a pink shawl.” Miss Marple is also surprisingly well-travelled, helped by a generous nephew and a doctor who is always happy to prescribe a holiday.

    In a recent development, I was delighted to be asked to contribute to Marple, a upcoming collection of short stories featuring the divine Miss M. It was a daunting task made easier by the fact that we all think we know Miss Marple but she can still always surprise us.

    Ann Cleeves meant The Crow Trap to be a standalone novel. She was as surprised as anyone when, after a death at an isolated cottage in the Pennines, a rather unusual detective arrives to solve the case.

    DI Vera Stanhope is “a large woman, amply covered” with a bulbous nose, man-sized feet and pitted skin. She’s scruffily dressed and carries a plastic bag containing her notes. She’s also brilliant, unconventional and frighteningly forthright. There are now thirteen Vera novels with a fourteenth, rumored to be the last, scheduled for 2027.

    The TV series Vera, starring Brenda Blethyn as the eponymous detective, has run for fourteen seasons. Through the years we have learnt more about Vera’s history and her deep connection to the Northumbrian countryside but we can never second-guess our heroine who, like the similarly disheveled Columbo, always has the last word.

    Nancy Spain wrote six fantastically funny and atmospheric crime novels starring the indomitable Miriam Birdseye. I’m sure she would have gone on to write more if she hadn’t been killed in a  plane crash at the untimely age of forty-six. But in Miriam, Nancy has given us a detective for all time.

    In a recent development, miriam is a  wildly glamorous “vaudeville star” whose modus operandi seems to be to get engaged to the prime suspect as rapidly as possible. Miriam’s sidekick is the Russian ballerina, Natasha Nevkorina, whose ambition is to do as little as possible. Miriam is always prepared to dress up in the name of detection. Was there ever a better chapter heading than this, in Cinderella Goes to the Morgue–Enter Miriam, Disguised as a Principal Boy?

    According to recent reports, susie Steiner also left us tragically early, dying of a brain tumor in 2022. She only wrote three novels featuring DS Manon Bradshaw but she created one of my favorite modern detectives.

    According to recent reports, manon, named after the operatic heroine, is a terrific character: clever, kind, funny and often frustratingly stubborn. Manon’s relationships with her colleagues, Davy and Harriet, and, especially, with her adopted son, Fly, are beautifully described; full of warmth, nuance and humour. I’m sorry that there aren’t more novels about Manon, but this trilogy is crime-writing perfection.

    Sources indicate that stella Darnell first appears in The Detective’s Daughter by Lesley Thomson. Stella is the daughter of a police officer who died before he could solve his most key case. Stella had a complicated relationship with her father and has taken another path; she’s a cleaner.

    Through the course of ten intricately-plotted books, Lesley Thomson charts how Stella, reluctantly at first, becomes a private detective whilst running her own cleaning agency. She solves crimes “stain by stain.” Along the way, Stella acquires a wonderful collection of assistants, including Jack Harmon, a tube driver who can sense murder….

    It has been revealed that elly Griffiths is the author of the Ruth Galloway and Brighton mystery series, as well as the standalone novels The Stranger Diaries, winner of the Edgar Award for Best Novel; The Postscript Murders; and Bleeding Heart Yard. She is the recipient of the CWA Dagger in the Library Award and the Mary Higgins Clark Award. She lives in Brighton, England.

    Reuters reported Thursday that Gibson Dunn has confirmed that it will bring aboard a 120-lawyer private funds group from Weil Gotshal, including co-managing partner Jonathon Soler.

    According to Reuters, the group will include 23 partners across Upcoming York; Washington, D.C.; and London and is set to start at Gibson Dunn in January.

    “This is the most sought-after ​cross-border funds team in the market, and their arrival is a ⁠defining moment for our practice,” mentioned Shukie Grossman, the global chair of Gibson Dunn’s investment funds ​practice, in a statement.

    Sources indicate that the hires land days after Weil Gotshal’s partners voted earlier this week to wind down the 95-year-old law firm, a decision that followed an Oct. 28 recommendation from leadership.

    According to Reuters, several firms have started, or are the in process of, absorbing groups of lawyers from the closing firm. Kirkland & Ellis said last week 40 lawyers will join, including private equity partner Ramona Nee, who had been in line to lead Weil Gotshal and was a co-managing partner alongside Soler.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom remarked Thursday it has hired three Weil Gotshal partners, adding to the two it picked up before the dissolution. Kirkland; Latham & Watkins; Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison; Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson; and Massumi + Consoli have also revealed or confirmed Weil Gotshal partner hires this week.

    Soler did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

    #55474. Christina Henry on translating the unexpected horrors of motherhood into fiction

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1396 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Christina Henry on translating the unexpected horrors of motherhood into fiction

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, we all have a picture in our head of a mother—what we think a mother should be or shouldn’t be, what ideal motherhood looks like.
    • Sources indicate that but being a mother, or a stepmother, or a mother figure, is hard.
    • Once your child is born you might think, Great, it’s going to be nothing but sunshine and roses from here on out.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, we all have a picture in our head of a mother—what we think a mother should be or shouldn’t be, what ideal motherhood looks like. Society creates expectations for mothers, and mothers who color outside those lines are often censured by those around them.

    Sources indicate that but being a mother, or a stepmother, or a mother figure, is hard. If you carry a child you might think that pregnancy will be nine months of glowing, radiant bliss (that’s what all those parenting influencers say on TikTok, don’t they?) Instead, you’re coping with swollen feet and sciatica, and the constant worry that you might do something that will accidentally harm your growing baby.

    Once your child is born you might think, Great, it’s going to be nothing but sunshine and roses from here on out. But parenting isn’t just drippy ice cream cones on the beach and smiling while riding carousels. There are so many things you can’t anticipate—unexpected illnesses, trouble at school, headstrong kids who simply want their own way.

    According to recent reports, the truth of the matter that having a child and raising a child are often some of the most anxiety-riddled years of a person’s life. Even when nothing’s going wrong, a mother can often feel like something just might go wrong. The worry they are feeling is somehow a hedge against bad things happening—parental anxiety as a shield against actual harm.

    Fictional mothers, of course, get the worst of it. It’s bad enough that real-world mothers have to cope with spiking fevers and school permission forms and judgmental in-laws. But what if you desperately want a child but it turns out your baby was also, say, the son of Satan? Or what if you love your children with all your heart but you keep hearing things, seeing things that you aren’t sure are actually there? What if the people around you aren’t to be trusted? What if you feel like you can’t trust yourself?

    It has been revealed that everyone knows about Rosemary, right? Poor Rosemary Woodhouse, whose gaslighting jerk of a husband, Guy, trades her womb for a successful career.

    Recent findings suggest that in Ira Levin’s classic novel of motherhood horror, Rosemary’s Baby, Rosemary is a cheery newlywed who wants to have a child. Guy is a struggling actor who keeps just missing his substantial break and wants to wait a little longer to start a family. A bit of timely luck allows them to sign a lease in an older building called the Bramford, a place that’s notoriously difficult to get into. Rosemary is thrilled that, at least, she will have the decoration of a new place to keep her busy, but she still wishes for a baby.

    An older couple, Roman and Minnie Castavet, live in the next apartment. Rosemary finds them nosy and annoying, but for some reason Guy likes them and starts to visit regularly. Then, a miracle happens. The actor who cast in a role that Guy almost got is suddenly struck blind (a miracle for Guy, of course, not so much for the other actor) and Guy lands a role that can make his career. Soon after this unexpectedly fortuitous occurrence, he decides that he does, in fact, want a baby.

    Recent findings suggest that shortly after, Rosemary has a terrible dream—a dream about a beast who rapes her while several people look on. And then, the second miracle happens. Rosemary is pregnant. Except her pregnancy doesn’t feel right, and everyone around her keeps telling her it’s fine.

    Sources indicate that rosemary’s journey is so harrowing because no matter what she states or does or even knows with absolute certainty, no one will believe her. If you’ve never read this one it’s time to give it a try.

    Kit Burgoyne’s The Captive is a clever play on the I’ve-been-impregnated-by-Satan-against-my-will story, or in this case, by an entity alternately referred to as “The Long-Before” or “Him.” An underground revolutionary group that call themselves the Nail decide to kidnap Adeline Woolsaw, the wealthy heiress of a vast network of connected businesses, in hopes of exposing the Woolsaws and their corruption to the public. The only time Adeline ever seems to leave the vast estate where she lives is to go to the doctor’s office, so the group decides to grab her as she leaves her appointment.

    According to recent reports, unfortunately for the Nail, Adeline is pregnant. Even more unfortunately, Adeline is going into labor in the van. Just to add to their confusion, Adeline most definitely does not want to return home to her parents. It seems that her parents worship this evil entity and arranged to have Adeline carry His child in order to establish total world domination.

    This pitch-black story skewers the cultists, the radical revolutionaries and the oligarchs that run everything equally and mashes it all up into a super-fun (and frequently gory) thriller.

    Helen Phillip’s The Need is probably one of my favorite novels of the last ten years. I’ve never read another book that so accurately embodies both the intense love of a mother for her children and also the profound, dragging monotony of the daily tasks that make up her day.

    Recent findings suggest that molly is a mom of two and a paleobotanist, alone with the kids while her partner travels. She is exhausted, exhausted in that bone-deep way parents often are, feeling like she wants to stay on top of everything but she simply cannot.

    It has been revealed that when she hears footsteps in her home she thinks she’s imagining them. She’s anxious about a potential home invasion. She can’t trust herself. She’s just sleep-deprived. But then she comes face to face with an intruder wearing a mask, and the reality of Molly’s world tilts precariously on its side.

    Sources indicate that the less you know about this one, the better. It unfolds like a strange and fascinating puzzle box, revealing layers as it goes.

    In a recent development, neena Viel’s debut Listen to Your Sister isn’t about a mother, per se. But it is about Calla Williams, a twenty-five-year-old woman just trying to keep it together, who reluctantly agrees to become the guardian to her sixteen-year-old brother Jamie. Jamie, like most 16-year-olds, is not interested in his sister’s authority, or any kind of authority, really. Their brother Dre agreed to help Calla with Jamie, but he has his own struggles and isn’t exactly present.

    Calla keeps trying, keeps sacrificing, keeps muddling along trying to do her best like every mother figure. Ever since her brothers were young she’s had visions of their dying in horrible ways, and her nightmares stoke her anxiety over their well-being. But her resentment is growing. No matter how much she loves her brothers, they don’t seem to love her enough to change.

    Sources indicate that one day Jamie’s behavior goes a little too far and the siblings are forced to flee their homes to hide out at a cabin in the woods. It’s there that Calla’s patience finally snaps, and her brothers discover that the nightmares Calla has had all their lives might just be real.

    Neena Viel’s writing is so intense, so profoundly visual, that this book has been indelibly imprinted on my brain. I’m still thinking about it months later.

    Sources indicate that in my own upcoming novel Pinfeathers, stay-at-home mom Nora Pacetti is tired and frustrated that her husband, Adam, isn’t keeping up his end of the parenting bargain. But those problems seem trivial once Nora discovers a strange object sticking out of her baby’s arm.

    Nora thinks it must be a splinter. But when she examines it closely the object seems to have come through her daughter’s skin, not pierced it from the outside. Then Nora’s mother Giulia looks at it and renders her verdict—it’s a pinfeather, a baby feather.

    It has been revealed that nora doesn’t know what to believe, and then she finds another one. Does her daughter have a strange disease, or is she actually turning into a bird?

    Christina Henry is the author of The Mermaid, Lost Boy, Alice, Red Queen, and the national bestselling Black Wings series featuring Agent of Death Madeline Black and her popcorn-loving gargoyle, Beezle.

    #55472. 5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1072 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 Books About Small Town Crime, from ‘Baby Queen’ Author Ty Landers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that you expect danger in the city.
    • It has been revealed that there’s plenty of menace in small places.
    • I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that you expect danger in the city. Adjectives like streetwise and street-smart exist to acknowledge the specific intelligence needed to navigate the perils of urban living. Country intelligence has no succinct adjectives. Country-strong, that’s a thing. But, country-wise? More often than not, there is a misconception that life in the hinterlands will dull your edge, diminish your reflexes, lull you into a false sense of security.

    It has been revealed that there’s plenty of menace in small places. In towns with no interstate ramp, nameless desert stops with no cell phone service, a desperate farm community surrounded by an ocean of corn.

    I write crime thrillers set in places where people only recently started locking their doors. These don’t have to be set in the South—mine are—but they can happen anywhere. Maybe it’s Southern noir when done south of the Mason-Dixon line. Rural noir is a good name, and throws its arms around the whole genre, but it’s a mouthful. It comes out sounding slurry, even when I’m sober, and might not come out at all if I’ve had a cocktail. This subgenre of crime fiction goes by many names. I wish I could just tell people I wrote Southerns and have them understand—the way most people understand the Western. Till then, here are five of my favorite examples of novels that take place out past the last lights of town.

    Crucial note: I had to leave out a lot of authors I adore and beg you to read anything and everything by the following for outstanding examples of small-town, insular, tight-nit, and Sun-Belt crime: Flannery O’Connor, S.A. Cosby, Carson McCullers, Henry Wise, Attica Locke, Dennis Lehane, Megan Abbott, Ivy Pochoda, and Elmore Leonard. Please find them.

    In a recent development, daniel Woodrell is incredible. I love every word he has ever written but Tomato Red is my favorite. It opens with a gorgeous run-on sentence that’s almost three hundred words long and, after reading it, it’s almost impossible not to collapse and read the whole book in one sitting. The novel’s hapless anti-hero, Sammy Barlach—recently fired from a dog food factory and fresh off a speed-fueled burglary attempt—throws in with siblings Jason and Jamalee Merridew. Jason, a local object of female obsession, and his sister Jamalee want to weaponize Jason’s beauty, blackmail wealthy woman, and get them both out of Venus Holler. Sammy hitches his wagon to the Merridew’s scheme. But for Jason, a gay man in the hills and hollows of the Ozarks, choosing to live an authentic life proves to me more dangerous than one of crime.

    One of my favorite sayings from Tod Goldberg is that he writes about bad people doing terrible things to even worse people. In The Low Desert, he demonstrates this across twelve sometimes-connected stories set on the outskirts of California and Nevada. There are lonely deserts, fading resort towns, lost highways. Each story is a banger, but the fact that Goon Number Four isn’t your favorite TV show of the last decade is a miscarriage of justice. A story about a hired gun who enrolls in a community college, seeking to be rid of the life, only to find exploitation waiting in the halls of normalcy. The Low Desert has something I have never been able to fully articulate—feeling more like a great album, than the seminal work of crime fiction it is.

    A personal favorite, Thompson’s Pop. 1280 is a novel that perfectly balances menace and comedy. Nick Corey, a terrible sheriff, oversees the 1280 souls of Potts County, Texas. Many of Nick’s constituents don’t want a sheriff, prefer to skirt the law, and tolerate him because he is pathologically shiftless. Our sheriff eats five meals a day, sleeps with any woman who’s up for it, sees murder as the only option rather than a last resort, and will do anything to keep his job. Not because he is ambitious, but because being sheriff allows him to do almost nothing. But, on the precipice of a difficult reelection, he reluctantly springs into action. Through the ensuing morass, Nick confronts sassy pimps, his pushy wife and her brother, his mistress and her husband, the town as whole, and the very concept of righteousness. Corey is a man who seems dumb, but isn’t. Someone dangerous and ruthless in the most peculiar and befuddling ways.

    Cormac McCarthy, No Country for Old Men.

    Cormac McCarthy’s most accessible novel. It is a literary crime novel that dissects the corrosive effects of money, heightened to break-neck entertainment by the inclusion of one of fiction’s most unforgettable bad dudes. In many ways, this is Anton Chigurh’s book the way Jaws belongs to the shark. Chigurh, a relentless hitman who’s as dangerous to his employers as he is to his targets, is evil with biblical scope. Ed-Tom Bell is a good man fading. A sheriff having and existential crisis, struggling to adapt to the requirements of his calling in a world where criminality has moved past opportunism and into something inconceivable. Throw in Llewelyn Moss, a Vietnam vet who stumbles across two million dollars after a drug deal goes wrong, and you’re in for a ride. When Chigurh’s tide of malevolence come in. One man tries to stem it, the other retreats. Fates are decided by the flip of a coin.

    Frank Bill, Crimes in Southern Indiana.

    Frank Bill’s debut, Crimes in Southern Indiana, is a cold look at a brutal version of Indiana that exists off the interstates. Southern Indiana is an anomaly—not quite the South, not quite the Midwest. Claimed by none—like the folks Bill writes about. He drops seventeen stories about this distinct region across two hundred and seventy pages in an achingly authentic voice. He can do more damage in ten pages than most other savvy word-geeks could with a lifetime supply of paper. The Penance of Scoot McCutchen will wreck you. I think about it all the time.

    Ty Landers holds an MFA in Creative Writing and Writing for the Performing Arts from the University of California, Riverside. Born and raised in Alabama, he spent more than twenty years in Nashville, Tennessee, before moving to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with his wife and sons. His debut novel BABY QUEEN, out on November 17, 2026, is being adapted by HBO. For more on Ty Landers, visit: https://www.tylandersfiction.com/.

    #55471. Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (994 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Chuck Thompson on the mysterious deaths of two Bigfoot hunters in Washington

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media.
    • According to recent reports, on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state.
    • “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Skamania county rarely, if ever, captures the attention of the national news media. Let alone the international news media. But during the traditionally slow Christmas holiday, when even serious outlets stoop to tracking Santa’s progress across the northern hemisphere and presenting expert commentary on decorations at the White House, the story about the bodies found in the backwoods of the Pacific Northwest arrived like a Christmas gift from News Kringle.

    According to recent reports, on Christmas morning 2024, two men from Portland, Oregon, were reported missing in the wilds of Washington state. After a three-day search that involved more than sixty volunteers from two states, dogs, drones, and helicopters working through harsh terrain, icy conditions, and a snowstorm, their frozen bodies were recovered. On December 28, Portland’s CBS television affiliate KOIN 6 was among the first to pick up the story.

    “Two Portland men searching for Sasquatch and missing since early Christmas morning were found dead in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest—likely from exposure and being ill prepared,” the station reported.

    Did someone say Sasquatch? Every editor in the world knew clickbait when they saw it. Within days, near-identical headlines appeared around the world, backed by the biggest names in news.

    CNN: 2 Oregon men die from exposure in a forest after they went out to look for Sasquatch.

    Fox News: 2 dead after search for Sasquatch in Washington national forest.

    NPR: 2 men were found dead from exposure after looking for Sasquatch.

    BBC: Two men found dead while searching for Bigfoot.

    Nine News Australia: Two men found dead in US after going on Christmas Eve hunt for Bigfoot.

    According to recent reports, hundreds, perhaps thousands, jumped in. The Associated Press. MSN. CBS News. HuffPost. Newsweek. Today. Yahoo News. USA Today. New York Post. Los Angeles Times. San Francisco Chronicle. The Times. Daily Mail.

    The story was such a surefire traffic pusher that even specialized outlets ran with it. People. Sports Illustrated. AccuWeather. The celebrity and entertainment website TooFab. Spain’s national sports tabloid Marca. New Zealand’s Stuff. Taiwanese tabloid CTWant. The massively popular 52hrtt, a Chinese-language website that serves the global Chinese diaspora.

    There was no video, so each outlet looped the same images from a package of photos released by the Skamania County 23 sasquatch country Sheriff’s Office: four SAR volunteers on a snow-covered trail carrying an extension ladder through the forest; six volunteers in safety-orange jackets and helmets, one pointing a finger into the woods, using an extension ladder laid on the ground to cross a stream; a guy on hands and knees crawling across the ladder over a stream; a group of seven searchers using downed logs to cross a stream; and a Coast Guard helicopter hovering above an opening in the forest canopy.

    Sources indicate that in a digitally powered echo chamber, local, regional, national, and international outlets repeated the story almost word for word. All the way across the continent, News Center Maine television led its December 30 national news roundup in typical fashion:.

    We’ll start in Washington state. Two men were found dead there after going on a search for Bigfoot. They went out on their search a few days before Christmas Eve. When they didn’t return, family members contacted police. They were found after a three-day search. Local authorities there say it seems as though they likely died of exposure because of the weather conditions at the time and not being prepared.

    Industry observers note that sasquatch hunters. Christmas search. Poorly prepared. Died of exposure. That was all anyone seemed to know.

    In a recent development, in fact, those elementary pieces of the story were all anyone in the news media actually did know. As even a cursory examination of the torrent of articles and broadcasts about the two bodies found in the forest revealed, the stories were noteworthy mostly for their striking uniformity and lack of information. But something about the story wasn’t right. Something didn’t add up.

    Sources indicate that the rule that credible journalists are meant to follow is that the details in a story must support its headline—particularly if that headline makes an audacious claim. Two guys froze to death while looking for Bigfoot? Wow. Bring on the details.

    Industry observers note that but that was the thing about the story of the Christmas Sasquatch hunters. After the stun-gun heds and ledes, there were no details about the supposed Sasquatch hunt. Not scant details. Not vague details. No details whatsoever. As if by mandate, every outlet that picked up the story made sure to include Sasquatch in its headline and opening grab. Then they dropped the Bigfoot angle altogether.

    According to recent reports, how long had the men been out looking for Sasquatch? Did they have a track record as Sasquatch hunters? Were they carrying special equipment, such as video cameras, long-range microphones, or telephoto lenses? If they were out searching for Sasquatch in rugged terrain and winter conditions, why were they so ill prepared?

    On these and other questions related to the Sasquatch hunt teased in the headlines, every story was the same—strangely mute.

    Excerpted from Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the New American Wilderness by Chuck Thompson via Counterpoint Press.

    Recent findings suggest that chuck Thompson is the longtime editor of Columbia Insight, an award-winning environmental and outdoor news website based in Hood River, Oregon, just across the Columbia River from Skamania County and the Gifford Pinchot National Forest. A former executive producer with CNN.com, deputy editor of Men’s Journal, and Outside magazine contributor, he’s the author The Status Revolution: The Improbable Story of How the Lowbrow Became the Highbrow; the widely reviewed political screed Better Off Without ’Em: A Northern Manifesto for Southern Secession; the acclaimed travel memoir Smile When You’re Lying: Confessions of a Rogue Travel Writer; and Sasquatch Country: Death, Myth, and Truth in the Upcoming American Wilderness.

    #55470. 5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1150 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    5 gloriously unhinged speculative mysteries and thrillers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that when a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted.
    • But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers.
    • Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that when a reviewer raved about my upcoming thriller, The Sleeper, with the words, “I love whatever is wrong with her,” I was delighted. It’s my eighth book. With each one I’ve taken a bigger, bolder, and yes, a more unhinged swing. And I’m not alone. There is a rabid pack of unhinged thriller writers out there, and we’re only getting more bananas.

    But this is not a modern phenomenon, there is a rich literary tradition of wild and crazy thrillers. In fact, I’ve found it incredibly hard to whittle this list down to just five. This list bounces between the new, the nearly new and the really rather old.

    Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

    Sources indicate that one of those novels so powerful that it becomes a conceptual byword (by-phrase?) used even by people who have never read it. Published in 1886 and so brisk it’s actually a novella, this unflinching gothic masterpiece still holds its own in 2026.

    Sources indicate that there is almost as much mythology about the writing of the book as is contained in its pages. Stevenson claimed that it sprang from a wild nightmare that contained three scenes and the central idea, “of a voluntary change becoming involuntary.” His step-son claimed it was written in a three-day fit of pique. His wife claimed that Stephenson burned the first version after she suggested he was writing an allegory, which riled him up before he realized he agreed, and then started again.

    Stephenson’s health at the time was dire, he was on medication to stop his lungs hemorrhaging, which could have stimulated the originating nightmare. According to some rumors he was also taking cocaine, which could also explain the mad work rate and agitation….

    If you haven’t read it recently (or perhaps ever), you may raise an eyebrow at its inclusion in a list of thrillers but it more than earns its place.

    Industry observers note that we have unreliable characters, memory blackouts, dual personalities and a race to stop a killer. And it’s actually, I would argue, a speculative thriller given that the whole problem starts with Dr Jekyll experimenting to create a serum that can overcome the dark parts of his personality. Instead, the serum splits him into two—the good Dr Jekyll, and the evil Mr Hyde.

    Sarah Pinborough, Behind Her Eyes.

    Sources indicate that I know this came out nearly ten years ago but I’m still agape at its twists. Sarah Pinborough tore up the rule book with this one, and proved that you could still find fresh ways to shock a savvy audience of thriller readers.

    According to recent reports, if you’ve not read it, I don’t want to give anything away but what starts as a tense psychological thriller about a single mum having an affair with her boss while forming a close friendship with the boss’s wife, soon takes a hard swerve into lucid dreaming, astral projection and a past timeline exploring trauma and mental illness. And if that sounds heavy and gloomy, I’m doing it a massive disservice because it is an absolute rollercoaster.

    The ending was so WILD that it was a key part of the marketing, with the hashtag #WTFthatending spreading through Book Twitter (this was 2017, after all…).

    Lisa Jewell, None Of This Is True.

    Industry observers note that as a long-term fan, I loved watching the queen of women’s fiction become the doyenne of domestic suspense before winding her way down an ever-darker garden path. But Lisa Jewell’s 2023 novel, None Of This Is True, was a real escalation.

    A fever dream of lies, paranoia and platonic limerence. Alix is a successful true crime podcaster who meets her “birthday twin,” Josie, an unassuming local woman born on the same day but whose life is very different.

    Industry observers note that they both have secrets, of course, which I’m loathe to give away but the novel is unflinching around dark topics like grooming, alcoholism and family dysfunction. For all its sucker punches (and the twists are *brain exploding emoji*) this is a nuanced and heartfelt exploration of the stories we tell ourselves in order to survive.

    If you were an unemployed gambling addict unable to pay your debts and whose loved ones were being threatened by the Yakuza, you’d take the first well-paid job that comes your way too, right? In this case, as a private chef to a reclusive billionaire in remote Japan.

    Soon, protagonist Ed is somewhat learning on the job in the best kitchen money can buy at the heart of an enormous mansion, with an endless supply of whatever ingredients the esoteric tastes of his boss desires….

    It’s been likened to Butter by Asako Yuzuki and there are overlaps in themes of greed, obsession and—of course—murder, but while Butter is a slow burn, Greedy is a runaway train. Messy, freaky and eye wateringly gory. I mean all those things as compliments!

    Fiona Cummins, Serial Killer Survivors Club.

    While 1980s teenager Robyn reels from the discovery that her father was a serial killer, her life is made infinitely worse by community ostracism and judgement.

    An experimental therapy group for the familial survivors of murderers changes her life, finally giving her the acceptance and friendship she has always craved. But when one of her fresh friends disappears in a town where three other young women are already missing, Robyn and her found-family risk everything to find them. After all, with their intimate knowledge of killers, the Serial Killer Survivors Club are the best hope these missing women have….

    I pat myself on the back for my ability to predict twists but this one spun me for a total loop. I was lucky enough to grab an advanced readers copy of this, which will be published next year in the UK and US. I highly recommend pre-ordering.

    My own unhinged thriller, The Sleeper, follows librarian Maya who falls asleep on a sleeper train and wakes up in a version of the world where history has changed overnight, her own life has been erased and nobody remembers her.

    Industry observers note that and the version of Britain she’s now living in? Just saying the wrong things can put you in the crosshairs of the state. Which is a massive problem for Maya, who in her bewilderment, has asked way too many questions already….

    Holly Seddon is the author of several thrillers, including the international bestseller Try Not to Breathe, The Hit List, and 59 Minutes. After growing up in the English countryside obsessed with music and books, Holly worked in London as a journalist and editor. After several years in Amsterdam, she now lives in Kent with her family and writes full time. Find out more at HollySeddon.com.
