    #55375. Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1575 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing.
    • In a recent development, until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a).
    • Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

    In a recent development, until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

    Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

    Section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

    In a recent development, eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

    For the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

    For the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”.

    As for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, said fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”.

    It has been revealed that the Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

    In a recent development, but a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

    Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

    For now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

    The 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

    It has been revealed that if the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

    According to recent reports, that is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process issue. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

    It has been revealed that rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

    Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

    Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks.
    • Recent findings suggest that the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec.
    • Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

    Recent findings suggest that the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

    In United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

    According to recent reports, in the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”.

    The challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”.

    In another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a New York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

    Trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”.

    The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

    Industry observers note that and in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the Latest York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

    Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

    Sources indicate that with only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi said, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

    Bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of New York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”.

    According to recent reports, when challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the New York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

    Sources indicate that in addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:.

    Sources indicate that one thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

    Industry observers note that finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    âIt is troubling to see a 21-times increase in ICE enforcement in these sensitive locations, especially when the Mayorkas memo did direct DHS to limit enforcement in these locations,â she said, referencing a Biden-era policy set out by former DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, who called sensitive location limits “fundamental.”.

    Mayorkasâ guidance did recognize “exigent” circumstances under which enforcement must take place, including during national security threats or risk of death, violence or physical harm.

    The second Trump administration’s day-one memorandum rescinded that guidance â along with a 30-year expected practice â and instructed federal officers to exercise discretion with a âhealthy dose of common sense.â.

    The districts argue the one-page memorandum offered no real explanation for abandoning the long-held approach, which was designed to encourage people to use essential services without fear of immigration enforcement.

    Sources indicate that âWhen you get rid of that constraint, common sense claims agents are going to be more likely to conduct enforcement actions,â Ouellette said. âRestoring that memo would redress that because it puts limits back in place.â.

    The government, meanwhile, claims both prior and current ICE guidance are mere policy recommendations, and that no such instructions have ever limited an agentâs statutory authority or ability to exercise discretion.

    Recent findings suggest that âThere has been increased enforcement action that plaintiffs and students, parents and teachers have found very concerning, and that has affected their decision-making,â Lundberg mentioned. âA change in the memo will not change that.â.

    She added that neither memo imposes any right on any member of the public.

    âIt does not confer any rights on immigrants that if you go to these sensitive locations that you are protected from enforcement,â she remarked.

    The districts note in court documents that arrests at sensitive areas jumped from 55 over the last two years of the first Trump administration to over 1,400 from January 2025 to April 2026 alone.

    That jump coincided with widespread absences â including a third of the districtsâ students staying home â and saw parents, teachers and staff arrested alongside children on school grounds and at bus stops.

    In a recent development, since Provinzinoâs preliminary injunction ruling, both the Fourth Circuit and the D.C. Circuit ruled in favor of sensitive area protections against ICE arrests on religious grounds.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A unanimous panel said the lower court lacked a sufficiently detailed record to bar enforcement of the law against nine major platforms.

    (CN) â A Fifth Circuit panel on Thursday lifted a second preliminary injunction blocking Mississippiâs Walker Montgomery Protecting Children Online Act, an age-verification and parental-consent law for social media platforms.

    Sources indicate that U.S. Circuit Judge Cory T. Wilson, writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, found internet advocacy group NetChoice failed to produce a sufficiently detailed record showing the statute is unconstitutional as applied to its membersâ specific sites and features.

    The panel determined the lower court erred by enjoining the law in its entirety as to nine NetChoice member platforms â including Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, X, Reddit, Snapchat, Pinterest, Nextdoor, and Dreamwidth â without conducting the intensive and specific analysis required for as-applied relief.

    âBecause the district court did not perform the fact-intensive analysis necessary to substantiate why the Act is unconstitutional as applied to each member website, and because it did not tailor injunctive relief to each member website, it erred in issuing the second injunction,â Wilson, a Donald Trump appointee, wrote for the panel.

    The panel determined general declarations claiming the lawâs requirements would be burdensome fell well short of the particularized evidence needed to craft a narrowly tailored injunction.

    Industry observers note that âSimply put, the district court had too little to go on in entering its second injunction â which included a complete bar on enforcement of the act as to nine covered platforms operated by NetChoiceâs members. Because the injunction was not narrowly tailored as applied to those sites, the relief entered by the district court was at least premature, if not unwarranted.â.

    Industry observers note that the panel remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Courtâs decision in Moody v. NetChoice and its own prior guidance in the case. Whether the statute ultimately violates the First Amendment remains an open question.

    Mississippi enacted the law in 2024 after the suicide of 16-year-old Walker Montgomery, who was targeted in an online sextortion scheme. The act requires covered interactive platforms to make commercially reasonable efforts to verify usersâ ages, obtain parental consent before allowing known minors to hold accounts, and implement strategies to mitigate listed harms to those minors. It also limits collection and use of minorsâ data and authorizes enforcement by parents or the attorney general.

    Sources indicate that âThe Walker Montgomery Protecting Children Online Act asks social media companies to make reasonable changes that a responsible corporate citizen should embrace,â Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch wrote in a social media post Thursday. âToday, the Fifth Circuit ruled unanimously against NetChoiceâs challenge to this law, delivering an important victory in our fight to keep our children safe in the digital age.â.

    According to recent reports, netChoice, a trade association representing major internet companies, first secured a facial preliminary injunction from a Mississippi federal judge in 2024. After the Supreme Court decided Moody, the Fifth Circuit vacated that order and remanded. On remand, NetChoice shifted to an as-applied challenge; the lower court again blocked the law as to the nine platforms.

    The Fifth Circuit stayed that second injunction pending appeal, and the Supreme Court left the stay in place.

    âWeâre disappointed in todayâs decision, but nothing in the ruling holds that [the act] is constitutional,â Paul Taske, director of the NetChoice Litigation Center, said in a news release. âJustice Kavanaugh has already said NetChoice is likely to win on the merits, and we are assessing all options to best preserve access to lawful speech in Mississippi. Today’s ruling is about procedure and paperwork, not about whether the state can force its residents to hand over their IDs before they are allowed to access speech online.â.

    According to recent reports, the Mississippi case is one of a series of NetChoice challenges to state laws requiring age checks or parental consent for minors on social media. Outcomes have been mixed. Courts have blocked similar measures in several states, but appellate panels have grown more skeptical of broad injunctions after Moody. The 11th Circuit recently vacated an injunction against Georgiaâs comparable law, and a divided Sixth Circuit revived Ohioâs parental-consent requirement, among other developments.

    PASADENA, Calif. (CN) â The federal appellate judge wanted to know if an immigration officer with an administrative warrant intends to arrest someone when stepping onto that personâs property.

    The question went to the heart of âknock-and-talkâ operations by the Los Angeles Field Office of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement â a policy a lower court in 2025 forbade after a lawsuit by immigrant groups. That court determined the government has no license to arrest someone during knock-and-talks: knocking on the door, getting the person to identify themselves and then arresting them. Instead, a judicial warrant is required.

    It has been revealed that the federal government appealed to the Ninth Circuit, and a three-judge panel heard arguments Thursday. It took the matter under submission.

    Sources indicate that U.S. Circuit Judge Milan Smith Jr., a George W. Bush appointee, said the law is clear: if the express intent is to arrest, officers canât use the knock-and-talk method.

    âThey can go with a warrant,â Smith said, âbut they canât use knock-and-talk.â.

    U.S. Circuit Judge Danielle Forrest, appointed by Donald Trump, noted an officer could only approach a home with the same reason someone in the public would have. Otherwise, they have no license to enter the property.

    âWhy am I wrong about that?â she asked.

    Arguing for the government, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Drew Ensign remarked the authority has existed since 1797. Special rules apply in certain circumstances, one of which is immigration. Administrative warrants, issued by a non-neutral party, can result in arrest.

    âAdministrative warrants are constitutionally permissible,â he added.

    Those warrants gave officers the ability to solicit consent to enter someoneâs property to enforce immigration laws. They donât violate the Fourth Amendment, Ensign noted.

    Forrest said the three-judge panel examined evidence in the record, which included declarations from noncitizens represented by the immigrant groups. They say theyâve had officers arrive at their homes and arrest them.

    If an officerâs intent is only to gather information, that falls within an implied license, Forrest added â meaning no Fourth Amendment violation would occur.

    âThe governmentâs own evidence shows that is not whatâs happening,â she said.

    Industry observers note that arguing for the immigrant groups, attorney Jeremy Kreisberg said forced entry into a home is a key aspect of the Fourth Amendment. The government must have a judicial warrant to enter a home and arrest someone. The lower court vacated the knock-and-talk policy. Now, the government wants it back but lacks sound reasoning to bolster its arguments.

    The panel also questioned the attorneys on the issue of standing, or whether the plaintiffs had the legal ability to sue the government.

    Kreisberg said the government has the addresses of people the immigrant groups have helped.

    âThey know weâre here without authorization. They know where we live,â Kreisberg noted, adding authorities will target them.

    âTheir argument is, sure, they know where they live, they can just not answer their door,â Forrest stated, explaining her version of the governmentâs argument.

    Recent findings suggest that kreisberg stated the constitutional violation occurs when the immigration officer enters someoneâs property to arrest them. Itâs irrelevant whether someone is wise enough to ignore a knock-and-talk.

    It has been revealed that ensign argued the plaintiffs needed to identify people who face harm to meet the standing requirement. Additionally, the immigrant groups have no standing in the case.

    Sources indicate that âIt was all past injury, not a threat of future, imminent harm,â Ensign added. âItâs a claim thatâs particularly unlikely to occur.â.

    That led Forrest to ask for a standard defining âfuture injury,â suggesting the identification of specific people.

    âWell, theyâve done that,â she stated, adding the government has peopleâs addresses. âWhy isnât that enough?

    Industry observers note that âThe government is saying, âWe want to do this. This is our official policy,ââ Forrest added.

    AI technology identified teen’s bag of Cool Ranch Doritos as gun, lawsuit claims

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Updated: In 2025, artificial intelligence technology used by the Baltimore County Public Schools to screen for weapons identified a bag of chips as a gun, resulting in local police cuffing and searching students, according to a lawsuit filed Tuesday by the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law.
    • It has been revealed that besides the county, the police department and the school district, Omnilert, which made the technology, is named in the Baltimore County Circuit Court complaint, filed Nov.
    • A spokesperson for the police department remarked in a statement it could not comment on pending litigation, and the school district told the ABA Journal that it did not have a comment.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 19, 2026, 11:07 am CST.

    Updated: In 2025, artificial intelligence technology used by the Baltimore County Public Schools to screen for weapons identified a bag of chips as a gun, resulting in local police cuffing and searching students, according to a lawsuit filed Tuesday by the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law.

    It has been revealed that besides the county, the police department and the school district, Omnilert, which made the technology, is named in the Baltimore County Circuit Court complaint, filed Nov. 17.

    A spokesperson for the police department remarked in a statement it could not comment on pending litigation, and the school district told the ABA Journal that it did not have a comment. It did reference an update shared with its school community after the incident happened.

    According to the revision, an Omnilert alert was issued at 7:04 p.m., and following a review by school safety personnel, it was canceled at 7:06 p.m. At 7:17 p.m., the school principal “contacted the school resource officer (SRO) and reported the alert. Because this alert was received after school hours, the SRO called the local precinct,” according to the update.

    All the plaintiffs were Black teenage boys, and they were waiting for one of their moms to pick them up from football practice, according to the complaint. Taki Allen, one of the youths, was eating a bag of Cool Ranch Doritos, and the Omnilert technology, which scans school security camera footage for firearms, identified the bag as a gun, according to the suit.

    At least six police cars arrived, some officers exited their vehicles with guns drawn, and they ordered the students to their knees. The youths were handcuffed and searched without being told what they were suspected of, according to the suit.

    No weapons were found, and one of the police officers reportedly muttered, “stupid AI cameras,” according to the complaint.

    And another officer, when he left, reportedly told the students, “Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem.”.

    According to recent reports, “We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” stated Damon Hewitt, the president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, in a Nov. 17 news release.

    Additionally, the suit alleges that some of the officers made light of the situation, with texts describing what happened, followed by laughing emojis. Causes of action listed in the complaint include unreasonable search and seizure, false arrest and imprisonment, gross negligence and improper conduct.

    According to recent reports, A spokesperson for Omnilert mentioned they are “truly sorry” for what the students and their families experienced. According to the company, the Maryland inspector general for education investigated their system and found no bias.

    “Our system is built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome. In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified. That is exactly why human review matters and why a canceled alert must stay canceled,” the spokesperson said.

    Updated Nov. 19 at 11:44 a.m. to include a response from Omnilert. Updated Nov. 19 at 1:05 p.m. with more information from the school district.

    #55360. Breaking: An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1320 w)

    Breaking: An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences.
    • Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct.
    • It has been revealed that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

    Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

    It has been revealed that the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

    According to recent reports, in two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”.

    In addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

    Within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

    Industry observers note that having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

    Recent findings suggest that last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

    The solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

    But the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead said he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

    Industry observers note that once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

    César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
    • In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
    • That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

    In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

    That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history shows that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

    Industry observers note that shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

    Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

    But this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

    Industry observers note that chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

    In a recent development, marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

    Justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

    It has been revealed that nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political problems as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

    And in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

    To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The Upcoming York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

    Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

    Shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of Upcoming York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

    In a recent development, justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

    Justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

    Industry observers note that again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

    Recent findings suggest that just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

    During Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to matter a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

    Sources indicate that when Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

    Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

    Industry observers note that in the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a latest story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

    In a recent development, if I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

    Regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

    Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.

    It has been revealed that recommended Citation: Mark Miller, The Supreme Court before it stood apart, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-before-it-stood-apart/.

At a predetermined point along the tracks, the burglars cut the air hoses that control the train’s brakes, bringing it to an emergency halt.

    Other crew members would be ready with trucks and vans to rapidly collect the boxes of shoes and other merchandise from the train and take them to their stash houses.

    Some crew members would contact buyers, including one unidentified retailer who repeatedly bought large quantities of Nike sneakers from the train robbers.

    In a recent development, “On July 14, 2025, at approximately 12:13 p.m., defendant Marquina offered to sell defendant a Organization 1 representative 600 pairs of Nike Air Force 1 sneakers for $60 each, claiming they retailed for $125 each,” the prosecutors wrote. “The Company 1 representative responded, ‘Iâll buy all air forces … Bring asap.’”.

    The next day, this defendant asked the organization to pay him in cash because the banks were âtripping.â.

    The crew wasn’t shy about flaunting their riches in selfies with stacks of stolen merchandise and cash, as well as making videos of themselves while burglarizing the trains.

    They also created a group chat on Instagram called “Los Trenes,” where they discussed their thefts as they were happening.

    “On July 15, 2026, at approximately 1:57 a.m., defendant Rodolfo Angel posted to the Los Trenes Group Chat, ‘Train still over there?’ At approximately 2:23 a.m., defendant Estrada posted, ‘Stopped it good,’ and defendant Sanchez replied, ‘Whoop,’” prosecutors stated in the indictment.

    The trains were stopped and robbed along tracks in industrial areas southeast of downtown LA and elsewhere in Southern California.

    The defendants are charged with conspiracy, theft of interstate railroad cargo, possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo and violence against railroad carriers.

    The court docket didn’t yet list lawyers representing the defendants.

But the government was back in court Thursday to ask a Ninth Circuit panel to reverse that order.

    âI think anyone would appreciate that the megaphone use at problem here was precisely the type of activity that would be likely to affect people working inside this office building,â Springer told the panel.

    But the judges also questioned how much discretion federal officers would have to enforce the regulations and whether the regulations could apply in different types of federal buildings.

U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung asked. “There’s a traffic jam, someone starts honking, people inside the federal building can hear it, they seem to be affected by a loud or unusual noise. Would that subject them? Would that be a violation?â.

And if the answer is no, why not?â.

    Marianne Dugan, representing the protesters who sued after the regulations were issued, argued that the exchange with the government attorney illustrated why the regulation was facially unconstitutional and could not be narrowed.

    Industry observers note that the regulation has a chilling effect on ordinary people who want to protest at federal buildings, she noted. Despite the preliminary injunction, a protester was threatened as recently as Wednesday with a citation, she added.
